articles.title: Pete Hegseth confirms cutting 20% of US military generals and admirals
articles.summary: Defense secretary ranted against diversity claiming ‘no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals’ in troops
articles.byline: Shrai Popat in Washington and Ariana Baio in New York

blocks.text: US defense secretary Pete Hegseth has confirmed plans to cut 20% of generals and admirals and declared “no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps” would be tolerated inside the country’s military.

Delivering his latest extraordinary attack on diversity, and dismissing reports of low morale within the US armed forces as “false claims”, Hegseth also suggested they were retaining service personnel at “record” rates.

The defense secretary pointed to those aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, following concern over mental health and supply issues on the aircraft carrier, which was deployed for almost nine months. Some “80% of the force” on board was retained, he said.
Addressing lower-ranking troops at the Marine Corps Base on Wednesday, Hegseth boasted about the anti-diversity policies in the Pentagon pushed by Donald Trump’s administration.

“The only focus, as you know, in your formations should be training, readiness, accountability, discipline and lethality,” Hegseth said. “And when you pursue those things, you don’t have to walk on eggshells … the complainers, the ideologues and the poor performers are no longer in the driver’s seat.”

He added: “But it’s worth saying again, so the fake news understands it. We are no longer the woke department or the weak department. Simple translation of that: no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors.”
Generals “who clung to the woke department, or seemed to think civilian control of the military is simply a suggestion, well, they no longer work here”, Hegseth said.
Eight US navy personnel assigned to the Lincoln attempted suicide since the start of their lengthy deployment as part of the US war on Iran, it emerged last week.

Hegseth appeared to reference the carrier while attacking the media on Wednesday, insisting there are “disingenuous headlines about deployment lengths, patently false claims of low troop morale, or flat-out propaganda, as if it’s written by our adversaries”.

The crew of the Lincoln, which was at sea for 286 days, disembarked on 1 September in a Thai resort city. The crew had been scheduled to wrap their deployment in May, but it was extended amid Trump’s war on Iran.

During his speech in Quantico, Virginia, the defense secretary announced several new initiatives, including a a new Pentagon project which will see Elon Musk, Palmer Luckey – a top Trump donor and ally – and Newt Gingrich, the former US House speaker, work with the department to study the “future of warfare”.
The Guardian previously reported on how Luckey’s company, Anduril Inudstries, a major defense technology company, has received billions in government contracts over the last year.

Hegseth also took aim at Ivy League universities and liberal arts colleges during his speech – which Trump has targeted routinely since he returned to office. The defense secretary branded the institutions as “DEI worshipping woke factories”. Notably, Hegseth is a graduate of Harvard and Princeton Universities – both members of the Ivy League.

Hegseth said the Pentagon would now partner with other institutions as part of its educational pipeline. Some of these schools, such as Liberty University and Hillsdale College, are known for conservative values.
Others joining the partnership are Louisiana State University, Mississippi University and Tuskegee University.

blocks.text: Telcos ready temporary disaster roaming before summer

blocks.caption: Josh Taylor

blocks.text: Josh Taylor

Telstra, Optus and Vodafone will from today be able to move users over to one of their rivals’ networks in areas where coverage has dropped out due to natural disasters such as cyclones, bushfires or floods.
The capability will mean users in those areas will still be able to call, message, and get basic access to the internet if the other network is up at no additional cost.
This is beyond the existing capability for networks to hand over emergency triple zero calls to other networks when the call can’t get through.
The industry has flagged there will be some scenarios - such as power outages – when switching will not be possible.
The switch-on for temporary roaming will be managed by the three carriers, and will happen automatically for customers when activated.

The temporary disaster roaming can be activated in up to three affected areas at the same time, with up to 15 mobile sites included per area, and activated for 24 hours at a time. The disaster areas must be at least 400km apart.
Metropolitan areas are excluded from the roaming arrangement.
Good morning, Nick Visser here to pick up the blog. Let’s get into Thursday.

blocks.caption: Henry Belot

blocks.text: Henry Belot

From today, children under nine years old with mild developmental delays and autism can access early intervention services through a program called Thriving Kids, which is administered by state and territory governments.

The change was announced by the Albanese government in August 2025 and will slowly move children off the National Disability Insurance Scheme. It will fully replace the NDIS for these children by 2028.
Unlike the NDIS, participation in Thriving Kids won’t require a formal diagnosis, potentially speeding up services and saving families money.
The health minister, Mark Butler, recently told parents there would be no gap in government support for their children.
Queensland is the sole Australian state refusing to sign on to the Thriving Kids program, leaving families in limbo as the first phase of the NDIS replacement scheme launches.
You can read more details about the change here:
ATO finds one-quarter of big firms pay zero tax

blocks.caption: Jonathan Barrett

blocks.text: Jonathan Barrett
More than one-quarter of big companies operating in Australia paid no income tax in 2024-25, according to the Australian Taxation Office’s latest corporate transparency report.
The report says companies mostly cited an accounting loss – when expenses outstrip revenue.

Guardian Australia has previously reported how some multinationals, including the Singtel-owned Optus and coal miner Adani, regularly pay no tax, citing infrastructure investments and operating expenses .
About 27% of entities in the report reported zero tax, which was a similar figure to the year before.
In total, 4,299 entities earning at least $100m in total income paid a combined $87.5bn in tax in 2024–25, led by Australia’s large mining sector.
The ATO acting deputy commissioner, Michelle Sams, says the agency is “increasingly focused” on making sure digital businesses and supply chains, including data centres, paid their share of tax.

double quotation markWe look very closely if there’s no tax being paid in significant industries, including things like data centres, to make sure that the level of tax being paid reflects the economic activity that’s happening in Australia.

articles.title: Pete Hegseth appoints Elon Musk to US taskforce on future of warfare
articles.summary:
A year after his explosive tenure at Doge, the SpaceX CEO is back in the Trump administration’s good graces

Pete Hegseth…

blocks.text: Pete Hegseth announced on Wednesday that Elon Musk will co-lead a government project to study the future of warfare, marking the SpaceX CEO’s first return to government since he ran the chaotic, so -called “department of government efficiency”, or Doge. Musk will be joined by Palmer Luckey, CEO of the defense tech company Anduril, and Newt Gingrich, the former Republican speaker of the House.

A defense department press release on the effort, called Project Meridian, described its goal as “identifying the capabilities required to achieve absolute technological dominance on the next-generation battlefield”. The project will run for 120 days and culminate in an unclassified public report of its recommendations.

The defense department’s project brings Musk back into government work a little more than a year after his explosive tenure as leader of Doge, which gutted federal agencies while failing to achieve its stated cost-cutting goals. It is also a sign of how Musk has re-entered the good graces of the Trump administration after a dramatic falling out with the president last year.

Unlike Musk’s role at Doge – which drew heavy public criticism and costly boycotts of his products – the scope and goals of Project Meridian appear as if they will be much less time-consuming for the tech mogul. The project intends to look at how the US military can utilize new technology and also carry out warfare in untested terrains including subterranean depths and on the moon, the defense department stated in its release.

“We are witnessing rapid advances in artificial intelligence, autonomy, directed energy, robotics, biotechnology, among other critical high-tech areas. Combined, these new domains, new ways of fighting, and technological developments will profoundly alter the character of warfare,” Hegseth said in a memo. “To maintain global dominance, the United States must anticipate future operational environments and act decisively to develop the tools to dominate in them.”

Musk and Luckey are far from independent arbiters of the future of warfare. Both have extensive defense department contracts through their companies, with Anduril’s business centered on the government purchasing products that it advertises as the latest advance in warfare.

Gingrich was appointed as a member of the defense policy board in December 2020 during the first Trump administration but was dismissed less than three months later after Joe Biden became president. Going back to the 1990s, he has been warning about the threat of an electromagnetic pulse attack that could knock out US power grids.

articles.title: Human rights panel condemns Canada's inaction regarding Indigenous people
articles.summary: Canada is failing to meet international legal obligations by refusing to hold thorough investigations into the crimes committed in its residential school system, says a global human rights…

image.caption: The Permanent Peoples' Tribunal judges, from left to right, Seanna Howard, Frances Webber and Valmaine Toki give preliminary conclusions following a week of hearings in Montreal in May. (Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Montreal·New

Canada is failing to meet international legal obligations by refusing to hold thorough investigations into the crimes committed in its residential school system, says a global human rights organization.
Final report released to coincide with National Day for Truth and Reconciliation
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Sep 30, 2026 5:14 PM EDT | Last Updated: 16 minutes ago
The Permanent Peoples' Tribunal issued its final report Wednesday, saying that the residential schools posed "widespread, systematic and most serious human rights violations."

Released to coincide with the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, the 78-page report urged Canada to investigate, prosecute and punish the perpetrators of these violations, and to provide reparations. The tribunal accused the country of doing "very little" to prevent the continuation of discrimination against Indigenous Peoples.

The judgment also condemned Canada for showing "deliberate … contempt" before the international community. It said the country refused to sign certain international conventions and modify its criminal law to include genocide, enforced disappearances and apartheid.
Recognition 'mostly deprived of practical effect'
Former prime minister Justin Trudeau and the House of Commons recognized in 2019 and 2022 that the operation of the residential school system constituted an act of genocide.
However, the tribunal's report called the acknowledgments "mostly deprived of practical effect by the extremely limited criminalization of genocide in Canadian domestic legislation.”

It also said those recognitions "have not had tangible consequences or been accompanied by any substantial change in the public policies of the successive governments regarding the treatment of Indigenous Peoples."

The tribunal reviewed extensive evidence gathered during its hearings last May. The evidence showed that some 15,000 Indigenous children were taken from their communities and sent to residential schools where they were forbidden to speak their language.
The children then faced poor living conditions, inadequate or nonexistent health care, malnutrition, forced labour, harsh discipline and punishment, and sexual abuse.
Continued discrimination, report says

Indigenous people face continued discrimination, namely through the forced and coerced sterilization of women as well as the removal of children from their communities by welfare services fuelled by a lack of support for Indigenous children both on and off reserves, said the report.

Drawing on the definitions in the International Convention on Genocide, the tribunal concluded that Canada failed to end and remedy the acts of genocide. It cited the Canadian government's refusal to fund and support the search for missing Indigenous children and their graves.
The judgment additionally accused Canada of "ongoing land theft and the criminalization of Indigenous land defenders by police and other government agencies."

The actions taken by Canada, the report states, amount to crimes against humanity, as defined by international conventions. These include the enslavement of children through forced labour, the forced transfer of population, severe deprivation of physical liberty, rape and other forms of sexual violence of comparable severity, forced sterilization, and persecution on racial grounds.
Apartheid system in place

It also concluded that Canada had a system of apartheid in place. The report defines apartheid as the institutionalization of segregation and discrimination against a subjugated racial group by a dominant racial group.

In its recommendations, the tribunal asked Canada to conduct thorough investigations into the disappearance and deaths of children in its institutions and that residential schools' archives and records be conserved.

items: Canada continuing genocide against Indigenous Peoples, international tribunal finds

blocks.text: It called on the government to provide financial support for research related to residential school burial sites, to commemorate and protect these sites, and to fund the revitalization of Indigenous languages.
All sacred objects held by governments, museums, national parks, and academic institutions should be returned to the communities to which they belong, it added.

Several recommendations focus on improving conditions on reserves, particularly in the areas of health and education. Others address respect for territorial rights and reparations for land dispossession.

Other recommendations target the Catholic Church and other religious communities who operated the residential schools, including reparations for stolen land and the restitution of these lands where former churches are located.

articles.title: Flydubai passenger describes putting attacker in chokehold after cockpit stabbing
articles.summary: Other passengers on the Israel-bound flight described the "terrifying" moment the plane dropped.

blocks.text: Passengers on a flight to Israel have recounted how they subdued a pilot after he stabbed the other pilot and appeared to be trying to disable the plane, while others described the "terrifying" moment they thought they would die.
Appearing in a bloodstained shirt after the ordeal, Yaniv Hayun told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu he realised something was wrong when the aircraft suddenly dropped.
The plane, en route from Dubai to Tel Aviv, plummeted 17,000ft (5,200m) in less than two minutes.
"Someone screamed... the light went out," Hayun said in a video posted by the prime minister on social media.
He and others tried to push open the cockpit door, but the pilot who had been stabbed was very close to it, so it was hard to open. Before he collapsed, the injured pilot managed to open the door.

When Hayun and another man entered the cockpit, he said he saw one pilot down and the attacker on the instruments, between the two seats, "trying to destroy the instruments in order to...disable the plane".
"I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and pulled him - first and foremost - outside," Hayun said.

"We pulled him out; it was a matter of seconds. I called out to the Israeli guys with us on the plane - I called them, and two other guys came over to me... we pinned [the attacker] down to keep him secure."
The Flydubai flight eventually landed at Tabuk airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia, and the passengers were later taken to Tel Aviv's Ben Gurion airport on a repatriation aircraft.
They were greeted by crowds of onlookers playing music, singing, dancing and waving Israeli flags.
"Thank God I'm alive," passenger Haim Lazarovich told journalists, adding that "the most terrifying moment in this flight was when the pilot loses control".
Oran Choen, an 18-year-old passenger, described the incident as "a very tough moment".
"Maybe it was five minutes, but it feels like hell - I heard my brother behind me scream that we was going to die," he added.
A paramedic from Israel's ambulance service later told the BBC that a number of people were "very emotional and crying as they came off the plane".
The stabbed pilot, Indian national Captain Smit Machchhar, was taken to hospital but is in stable condition, according to the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia.
Netanyahu praised Machchhar as a "true hero" of "extraordinary bravery".
The attacker was arrested and is being questioned by Saudi authorities.
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has called it an "attempted jihadist terror attack". No official motive for the incident or further information has been given.

articles.title: Pentagon confirms U.S. military will cut 20% of generals and admirals
articles.summary: U.S. War Secretary Pete Hegseth confirmed Wednesday that the U.S. military will cut 20 per cent of its generals and admirals as he made a series of announcements in what he called his "state of the…

image.caption: U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth confirmed more cuts to admirals and generals of the U.S. armed forces during a speech at Marine Corps Base Quantico Wednesday. (Alex Wong/Pool/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

U.S. War Secretary Pete Hegseth confirmed Wednesday that the U.S. military will cut 20 per cent of its generals and admirals as he made a series of announcements in what he called his "state of the force" address.
War Secretary Pete Hegseth called the cuts 'accountability and long overdue'

Hegseth was speaking to junior officers and enlisted leaders at the Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia, the second year in a row that he has given such an address. This time, the U.S. military is seven months into a war with Iran with no clear end in sight, has captured Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and killed more than 200 people in strikes on alleged drug trafficking boats in Latin America, among other actions worldwide.
The speech is not a usual fixture among Pentagon leaders. While Hegseth's predecessors have regularly addressed troops and top officers, they have traditionally done so in small or private settings.

The Pentagon chief, however, again led with how he has drastically retooled the U.S. military by targeting what he calls "woke" culture — through a rollback of diversity programs, a review of ground combat units with female troops and a new screening program for "testosterone deficiency" among male personnel.

Pentagon officials had previewed that Hegseth would announce more cuts to the number of generals and admirals. He directed all military services to double the 10 per cent reduction he ordered last spring for roughly 800 flag and general officer positions, making it a total 20 per cent decrease to be completed by Jan. 1, 2027.
"I call it accountability and long overdue," he said.
New drone-focused warfare command

The Pentagon chief announced the creation of a new four-star command to oversee the rollout of autonomous and robotic capabilities in what he called "the fastest peacetime shift in modern military history."

The rollout comes a month after officials said an army unit based in Europe that specialized in drone warfare had been directed to return to being a traditional infantry battalion, ending its efforts to learn and use the battlefield technology.

A bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers subsequently asked the army to explain the order, given that the world's battlefields are rapidly evolving and military tactics increasingly rely on uncrewed systems to fight.

items: Several U.S. military bases, diplomatic buildings have been damaged in Iran war: inspector general report
Pentagon makes testosterone screening mandatory for U.S. service members effective immediately

blocks.text: The announcement of the new drone command comes with the U.S. in a stalemate with Iran over control of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital energy shipping corridor. The war has forced U.S. forces in the region to expend hundreds of expensive missile interceptors to defend against Iran's missile and drone attacks, which have still managed to kill and wound U.S. troops.

Hegseth repeated claims that the U.S. military has destroyed Iran's navy, air force and defence systems as well as many of its leaders and its industrial base. But the Islamic Republic has continued intermittently to launch drone and missile attacks against U.S. or allied bases in the region, while maintaining its ability to strike commercial and military ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

During his speech, Hegseth touted the Trump administration's major investments in the defence industry and push for contractors to speed up their work to expand the nation's weapons arsenals. But experts say U.S. military contractors will need at least three years to replenish stockpiles of key weapons systems used heavily in the Iran war.
Criticism over cuts to general ranks

Members of Congress have criticized the war and the drawdown of munitions stockpiles, and some called the latest cuts to the general ranks a "purge" of the military's top ranks that will take years to rebuild.

"He's got some kind of like deep-seated grievance about leadership in the military," said Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly, a former Navy combat pilot and NASA astronaut, who has been critical of Hegseth. "He's purging a generation of great leaders of the military, and it's going to take a generation to recover from it."
Republican Sen. Mike Rounds, a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said he wanted to understand Hegseth's reasoning behind the decision.
"If it's simply a matter of eliminating a very heavy top, there may be some validity to it, but I want to see it first," Rounds said.

Randy George, a move that angered both Republicans and Democrats in Congress. The departures also have included a number of senior officers who are women or people of colour.

articles.title: Senate blocks Republican bill restricting stock trades by US Congress members
articles.summary:
Democrats block measure they say didn’t go far enough – and was bundled with ‘poison pill’ voter ID rules

The US Senate on Wednesday blocked a Republican bill restricting stock trading by…

blocks.text: The US Senate on Wednesday blocked a Republican bill restricting stock trading by members of Congress, after Democrats refused to advance a measure they said would let lawmakers keep their portfolios and was bundled with voter ID rules they called a “poison pill”.

The 53-47 vote fell seven short of the 60 needed to open debate on the Stop Insider Trading Act, which the Republican-controlled House passed in July. Every Democrat and independent voted no, and the failure comes five weeks before the 3 November midterms.

The bill would bar members of Congress, their spouses and their dependent children from buying individual stocks. Democrats said that falls short of a ban because lawmakers could keep everything they already own, reinvest dividends into more shares and let a spouse or child trade on their behalf.

Several also wanted the rules extended to the president and other White House officials, while others objected to the photo ID requirements for voting, which they said would make it harder for eligible citizens to cast ballots.

Chuck Schumer, the Senate Democratic leader, called the bill “a permission slip for corruption” and said Republicans had designed it to fail. He noted that a Senate committee advanced a bipartisan ban last year and accused Republicans of ignoring it. His deputy, Dick Durbin, dismissed the “meaningless” bill as “an inadequate congressional stock trading ban” and “Republican messaging”.

Republicans said Democrats had picked politics over reform. Nebraska’s Pete Ricketts, who faces a tight re-election race, said on the Senate floor “we need to restore the faith of the American people” in Congress.

Joe Gruters, chair of the Republican National Committee, accused Democrats of choosing to “protect the swamp” over voter ID and accountability and said “voters should hold them accountable in November”.

The fight is the latest in years of failed efforts. The best known is the so-called “Pelosi Act”, introduced by the Republican senator Josh Hawley of Missouri, who said it would help restore trust in Congress by banning members from trading and holding stocks. A Senate committee advanced a reworked version 8-7, with Hawley the only Republican in favor, after the name was dropped and future presidents were added, though Trump was shielded. Trump attacked Hawley on Truth Social over the vote, and the bill never became law.

Trump’s own trading has been eye-popping. The Democratic senator Elizabeth Warren and California representative Robert Garcia pointed to disclosures showing more than 14,000 stock trades in his first year back in office, worth up to $1.06bn, calling the volume “unprecedented” for a sitting president. Bloomberg reported that from January 2025 to June 2026, Trump made nearly 28,700 trades, compared with 22,200 by all lawmakers combined. Nothing in the filings shows insider trading, and they do not say whether Trump directed the trades himself.
Lawmakers have faced similar questions, and a report by Common Cause found members of both parties made 13,324 trades worth $635.6m last year.
In April 2025, Marjorie Taylor Greene, the former Republican US representative, bought shares in Apple and Tesla just before Trump paused many of his tariffs and markets surged.

Nancy Pelosi is one of the most closely tracked traders in Congress, and Trump called her out by name in February’s State of the Union speech. Yet Republicans and Democrats were evenly split among the 10 best-performing portfolios in Congress last year, while Pelosi ranked 28th, according to an analysis by Unusual Whales.
The vote was among the Senate’s last acts before it breaks for the rest of campaign season.

articles.title: In-laws charged with murder of New York Times games engineer in California
articles.summary:
Shili Chen and Shouyong Zhang, both 77, charged days before Jonathan McKinsey and wife were set for hearing in divorce case

A California couple have been charged with murder after…

blocks.text: A California couple have been charged with murder after authorities say they shot their son-in-law to death Saturday in a public park, days before he and the couple’s daughter were set for a hearing in a bitter divorce case.

Shili Chen and Shouyong Zhang, both 77, were due in court Wednesday for an arraignment on the charges. The Associated Press was not able to reach an attorney for the couple prior to the court appearance. Their daughter, Candice Jang, could not be reached, though she appeared virtually at Wednesday’s hearing.

Jonathan McKinsey, a 40-year-old gaming engineer for the New York Times, was shot dead in the parking lot of a sports complex in Dublin, east of San Francisco. A police sergeant was driving nearby and saw him on the ground as witnesses began calling 911 and pointing out the couple in their vehicle, who were still near the scene, Dublin police said in a news release.

Police detained the couple as they were driving away in the parking lot. Prosecutors said Zhang admitted to shooting McKinsey during a later interview, and a firearm was found in his car that he admitted to using during the crime.
Prosecutors also said surveillance video was recovered showing Chen and Zhang shooting the victim “in concert”.
Chen and Zhang’s murder charges included additional allegations of lying in wait and using a firearm.

Court records show McKinsey’s killing came during a contentious divorce with Jang and a custody battle over the couple’s three young children. In petitions for restraining orders filed last year, the couple accused each other of physical, emotional and psychological abuse going back more than a decade. McKinsey, who is transgender, alleged that both Jang and her parents were verbally and physically abusive regarding a gender transition he underwent years ago.
The killing occurred a week before a hearing was scheduled in McKinsey and Jang’s divorce case. The couple had been married since July 2011.

McKinsey joined the New York Times in January 2023. He was director of engineering for New York Times Games and based in the San Francisco Bay Area, the paper said. A spokesperson declined to comment further.

articles.title: 'A trip down memory lane': N.S. man reunited with wallet lost 51 years ago
articles.summary: Carpenter Matty Goldsmith discovered a wallet last week in Dartmouth N.S., returning a time capsule of 1970 memories to its long-lost owner.

image.caption: Richard Gilroy was excited to reclaim his wallet lost in 1975, with everything in it fully intact. (Submitted by Donna Gilroy)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia
Carpenter Matty Goldsmith discovered a wallet last week in Dartmouth N.S., returning a time capsule of 1970 memories to its long-lost owner.
Social media successfully brought about a lost-and-found reunion spanning half a century
An accidental discovery at a house renovation site in Dartmouth, N.S., and a social media post have reunited a wallet lost 51 years ago with its owner.

While renovating a house for his company on Victoria Road, carpenter Matty Goldsmith found a wallet under the old floors containing identification documents including a driver's licence and student ID, as well as a 1975 theatre ticket for Hamlet and a dollar bill.
Goldsmith and his colleagues were surprised that everything was fully intact, and they guessed that the owner was a high school student who used to work there as a construction labourer.
"I decided like, why not try our luck with the internet and see if we can track this person down," he said.
His post quickly drew responses from the community, including owner Richard Gilroy's wife. Three days later, they met up and returned the wallet to Gilroy.
"I was very surprised to say the least," 68-year-old Gilroy told CBC News on Wednesday. "I'm very pleased to get it all back."
Although Gilroy remembers when and where he lost the wallet, his memory of what's inside has faded.
"It's very interesting that my original handwritten birth certificate was in my wallet, and I have no idea why my parents would have even given it to me,” Gilroy said.
As for the Hamlet ticket, he had no recollection of having seen the play, but said the $1.50 ticket price is "amazing."
Gilroy said he's thankful for Goldsmith, and he's planning to frame everything in his wallet to put on display.
Time capsules
Goldsmith said his job often brings him "little treasures and time capsules."
He once found some letters written in Chinese in a Vancouver renovation site, and a bottle of cobra whisky.
But this is the first time he uncovered someone's ID. Goldsmith said he quickly realized it's a long-lost item.
"It's always neat to think about like who left this here or what their life was like," he said.
He said it was pleasant to meet with Gilroy and his wife, and Gilroy was excited to "have that little piece of his past back in his hands."
"He was able to have a bit of this luck and get this time capsule," Goldsmith said. "It was such a nice trip down memory lane for him."

articles.title: Five EU states plan first deportation center in Africa for 2027
articles.summary: Greece, Germany, Austria, Denmark and the Netherlands are moving forward with plans to establish deportation centers outside the EU. An African partner country has reportedly already been selected.

image.caption: Prospective migrants who arrived in Greece are taken into a migration hubImage: Sofia Kleftaki/DW

blocks.text: Deportation centers are legally contentious, expensive and the subject of political controversy: For years, Brussels has been grappling with the issue of establishing such centers outside the EU for rejected asylum seekers. Previous attempts have failed due to legal objections, but now, a "group of five" consisting of Greece, Germany, Austria, Denmark and the Netherlands believes it has overcome these hurdles.

During an interview with the Greek television channel ANT1, Greece's Minister of Migration, Thanos Plevris, stated that the first of these so-called "return hubs" is scheduled to begin operations as early as the second half of 2027 — just in time for Greece to assume the EU Council Presidency.

Plevris said Greece had chosen an African country but could not reveal its name yet. Diplomatic circles and media outlets close to the EU have repeatedly cited Rwanda or Uganda, but neither country has been confirmed as the location.
No sealed detention centers
"We are not talking about centers in the sense that someone whose asylum application is rejected is sent to a closed facility in a third country," Plevris said.
The plan was rather to establish "open facilities" while the final return to the actual country of origin is being organized, he added.

The responsibility for the transferred individuals will not be transferred to the African partner country in order to prevent legal action for human rights violations, but will remain with the five participating EU member states. The EU "group of five" will also finance the project entirely on its own.

There are also plans for international organizations such as the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) or the International Organization for Migration (IOM) to monitor operations to ensure that international human rights standards and principles of international law are upheld.

blocks.caption: The British Supreme Court eventually stopped the push by the Conservative government to permanently deport prospective migrants to RwandaImage: Toby Melville/PA Wire/empics/picture alliance

blocks.text: Various attempts have been made in recent years to outsource asylum proceedings or deportations to countries outside the EU. None of these models worked as planned. All failed due to legal impediments, changes in government, or high costs. Below are some of the best-known precedents.
The British "Rwanda Model" (2022–2024)

The United Kingdom, under the Conservative government of Boris Johnson — and later under Rishi Sunak — sought to permanently deport migrants who had entered the country irregularly via the English Channel to Rwanda so they could undergo their asylum proceedings there.

However, the British Supreme Court ruled the plan illegal, finding that there were substantial grounds for believing that asylum seekers sent to Rwanda faced a real risk of refoulement — being returned to countries where they could face persecution or other inhumane treatment.

Prior to that, the British government had spent £715 million (€835 million/$966 million) in taxpayer funds on the Rwanda partnership and related implementation costs. In return, a total of four people had voluntarily relocated to Rwanda

blocks.caption: Migrants in Italian return hubs in Albania had to be returned to ItalyImage: Alketa Misja/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Italy's Albania model (in place since 2024)

Under Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, Italy signed an agreement with Albania to transport migrants intercepted in the Mediterranean directly to Italian-run centers established in Albania where expedited asylum proceedings could be conducted.

However, immediately after the camps opened, Italian courts halted the relocation. Judges argued that countries of origin such as Bangladesh or Egypt should not be classified as "safe" outright if certain groups face persecution there. These first migrants had to be returned to Italy immediately.

Italy is now using one of the camps solely as a deportation center for men whose asylum applications in Italy have been definitively rejected. Since the facility was converted in March 2025, only about 500 people have been sent there. By 2028, this comes at an estimated total cost of more than €670 million ($775 million).
Denmark's stand-alone initiatives (2021–2023)

In 2021, Denmark passed a law intended to allow asylum seekers to be flown to third countries outside the EU. Copenhagen engaged in intensive negotiations with Rwanda regarding a dedicated reception center. However, the European Commission and human rights organizations sharply criticized the initiative. In early 2023, the Danish government put the negotiations with Rwanda on hold. It became clear that the Danish plan was virtually impossible to implement legally and logistically. The government subsequently moved toward pursuing third-country return arrangements in cooperation with other European countries.
Changing legal framework

According to previous EU law, deportations to third countries often failed as courts required that a migrant have a personal connection to that third country, whether through language skills, relatives living there or a previous stay. The revised European asylum law, however, now allows individuals required to leave the EU to be transferred to a safe third country without a prior personal connection in certain circumstances — provided there is a corresponding agreement or arrangement with the third country.

A further basis for this new joint effort is the EU Return Regulation, agreed upon politically on June 17, 2026 by the Council and European Parliament. However, the regulation has not yet been formally adopted by the Council. Unlike before, the new legislation is an EU regulation and no longer merely a directive. As a result, it will apply directly once it enters into force in the EU member states bound by it. The regulation thus establishes a common EU framework for such return centers.

Furthermore, according to the new plans, the entire asylum procedure will no longer be outsourced to non-EU countries. The United Kingdom and Italy rejected this proposal. Instead, these "return hubs" will serve solely as transit stations for individuals whose asylum applications have already been legally rejected while they are financed and monitored by EU member states.

blocks.caption: Will Italy return to its migration hubs in Albania once the new EU migration pact is in place?Image: Filippo Attil/Chigi Press Office/Zumapress/picture alliance

blocks.text: Inadequate oversight and high costs?

Supporters hope that these measures will undermine the basis for human rights lawsuits regarding permanent asylum protection. Critics such as Doctors Without Borders and Amnesty International still see significant risks: They doubt that independent oversight, effective legal representation and medical care can be fully guaranteed in the hubs. They also fear that third countries could still deport people to their unsafe home countries without proper assessment.

Furthermore, experience to date shows that the construction and security of such centers, as well as the transport of those affected, often costs hundreds of millions of euro, and only a small number of people actually end up being returned.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Israeli forces overwhelmed by violent settlers in ‘terrorist attack’ on Palestinian family
articles.summary:
Settler violence in West Bank makes everyday life ‘untenable’ for Palestinians, says ICRC after assault on family trying to return home in Jalud

The International Committee of the Red Cross…

blocks.text: The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has said Israeli settler violence in the West Bank has made everyday life for Palestinians “untenable”, as a mob attack on Palestinians trying to return home prompted one of Benjamin Netanyahu’s main rivals to warn of a campaign of settler terror.

More than 100 militant settlers overwhelmed Israeli security forces early on Tuesday to attack a Palestinian family as they attempted to reclaim their homes which had been seized by settlers in the West Bank village of Jalud. Three Israeli security officials were injured and houses were set on fire.

The impotence of the Israeli military, the scale of the assault and the injuries inflicted on Israeli security officers by settlers prompted unusually harsh condemnation from Israeli politicians and commenters.

Israel is facing unprecedented international pressure over surging violence in the occupied West Bank, where settler militants backed by cabinet ministers have accelerated a campaign of ethnic cleansing ahead of Israel’s elections next month.

Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, condemned the attacks in Jalud as a “moral stain”. Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief and Netanyahu’s leading challenger in the upcoming elections, called for action to halt a “campaign of terror and violence”.
Deadlier attacks by Israeli settlers, including ones targeting Palestinian children, have drawn less attention inside Israel.

“Palestinian rights or safety are not the concern, even for people who are in the opposition,” said Mairav Zonszein, a senior analyst on Israel-Palestine with International Crisis Group. “The settler violence is an issue [for them] because it’s making Israel look bad, and also the idea that the military is losing control.”

blocks.caption: A Palestinian family were attacked as they attempted to reclaim their homes which had been seized by settlers in Jalud. Photograph: Atef Safadi/EPA

blocks.text: The ICRC said attacks, settlement expansion and severe restrictions on movement were making everyday life untenable for Palestinian civilians, who Israel has a responsibility to protect under international law. .

“The frequent and severe violence must be brought to an end,” said Julien Lerisson, the head of the ICRC’s delegation for Israel and Palestine. “What international humanitarian law says on the protection of private and public property, and on the population’s access to essential services, must be respected.”

A bar on imports of settlement goods came into force in the Netherlands last week, the UK has announced plans for even broader controls on trade and financing of settlements, and a similar bill will be introduced in the US legislature on Thursday.
On Tuesday, a Senate bill demanding a human rights report on Israel’s occupation of the West Bank was narrowly defeated after winning backing from all but one Democrat.

“Tonight a disaster was averted, but the barrier has been broken,” the Israeli analyst Roy Sharon wrote on social media after the vote, warning that “anarchy in the West Bank” may cost Israel military aid from the US and its international legitimacy.

A cartoon in Israel’s largest-circulation newspaper, Yedioth Ahronoth, on Wednesday showed two soldiers watching an arson attack on a Palestinian home. “They’re going to ruin my trip to Amsterdam,” one says to the other.

More than 60 Palestinian communities in the occupied West Bank have been wiped off the map since October 2023 and 18 others have been partly displaced, according to the Israeli rights group B’Tselem. Nearly 5,000 people have been forced from their homes, almost half of them children.

blocks.caption: Mahmod Tubasi, 60, and his wife, Aedah, 51, and their family had been forced out of their homes this summer by settler militants.  Photograph: Ammar Awad/Reuters

blocks.text: The Tubasi family, whose homes were burned in Jalud, had been forced out this summer after a weeks-long siege by settler militants. Last week they secured a high court ruling ordering the Israeli state to evict settlers and secure their return.

Late on Monday the Israeli military told the family that about 15 military police officers would escort them home immediately, Israel’s Haaretz newspaper reported. That was a small number given that Israel is celebrating the Sukkot holiday. The number of violent extremists in illegal settlements usually rises during festivals, and the force was outnumbered by a violent crowd within minutes of arriving.

“To carry out an operation such as this, and during the holiday of Sukkot when the [settler] outposts are packed, is madness,” a security source said. The military had not informed national police and the Shin Bet domestic intelligence service of their plans, so they had no security backup.

Settlers attacked a house when the Tubasi family arrived, forcing them to the roof, before the military decided to evacuate them in armoured military vehicles. The crowd then set the homes on fire, blocked roads and threw stones at Israeli security forces, injuring three personnel.

The two houses “were damaged beyond description”, said Wael ​Tubasi. “They damaged everything – the doors, the tiles were removed, the stairs were removed. They smashed the bathrooms, doors and windows. They left nothing, everything was broken,” he told Reuters.

blocks.caption: The Tubasi family’s homes were ‘damaged beyond description’, said Wael Tubasi. ‘Everything was broken.’ Photograph: Ammar Awad/Reuters

blocks.text: Earlier this year the former prime minister Ehud Olmert called for the international criminal court to intervene to stop settler violence because the state had failed.

Netanyahu condemned the “violent riots” and called for prosecution of the attackers, but defended the illegal settler movement. “The handful of rioters are not representative of the law-abiding settler public in Judea and Samaria,” the prime minister said, using an Israeli term for the occupied West Bank.
A landmark 2024 ruling from the UN’s international court of justice found that the occupation violated international law, a position the British government has endorsed.
An Israeli military spokesperson said two suspects had been detained, and called for action to tackle settler militants who targeted Israeli security forces.

“The violence directed at soldiers while they were carrying out their duties crosses a clear red line and is unacceptable,” the spokesperson said. “There is no place for such incidents in the state of Israel, and they must not be allowed to become the norm. Such phenomena must be addressed at their root.”

On Wednesday, some in Israel questioned whether the army and the state had the capacity to do that. “We have to look reality squarely in the eye: this was a terrorist attack and a failure by the Israeli defence establishment in its entirety,” Avi Ashkenazi wrote in the Maariv newspaper. “It is clear at this point that the real sovereign in Judea and Samaria are the extreme rightwing terrorist activists.”

articles.title: Pentagon says it has formally completed withdrawal of US troops from Iraq
articles.summary:
Twelve years after US mission against IS began, Trump hails ‘great day for America’ and calls war a ‘quagmire’

The Pentagon has announced it has formally completed its withdrawal of US…

blocks.text: The Pentagon has announced it has formally completed its withdrawal of US troops from Iraq, two years after the withdrawal was agreed to and 12 years since the US mission to fight the Islamic State started.
After the announcement, Iran and its allies celebrated the departure as a victory, while Iraqi security experts worry that the withdrawal could give IS and others a chance to recover.

“Today, the United States and our coalition partners formally concluded Operation Inherent Resolve in Iraq,” the Pentagon said in a statement, adding that the departure of its forces “marks the successful conclusion of the military mission that defeated Isis in Iraq”.
The Pentagon said it would continue to provide training and intelligence support to Iraq “to ensure Isis can never reconstitute from Iraqi territory.

“The primary responsibility for addressing Iraq’s remaining security challenges, including Isis remnants and Iran-aligned militias that undermine Iraqi sovereignty and regional stability, now rests with the government of Iraq.”

Speaking on Wednesday about the withdrawal at a White House event for Hispanic Heritage Month, Donald Trump cast it as a win, calling the Iraq war a “quagmire” that grew out of “very bad decision-making”. He said: “This is a great day for America.”
He also described it as a victory for both countries, saying it was “a victory for Iraq, and a decisive victory over Isis”.

Trump claimed credit for defeating IS, saying: “I decimated them and took them out in my first administration.” He said his administration “refused to let a temporary presence become a permanent one”, adding that he “felt, without question, it was time for America to go home”.

Trump contrasted the exit with Afghanistan, where he said equipment was left behind, insisting that this time US forces took everything. “I want every screw taken,” he said. “We came to fight a caliphate, and there is no longer a caliphate, so we are going home indeed.”
He also praised Iraq’s new prime minister, whom he said he endorsed during the Iraqi election campaign, saying he hoped he would “do a fantastic job”.
The US invaded Iraq in 2003 to oust its dictator, Saddam Hussein, who ruled the country for nearly 24 years.
The invasion led to hundreds of thousands of civilian deaths, civil war and sectarian violence in Iraq, as well as the rise of the IS militant group.

In 2011, Barack Obama declared an end to the Iraq war and announced that all US troops would be withdrawn from the country by year’s end. At that moment, the US military presence in Iraq stood at under 40,000, and 4,400 US military members had been killed.

But in 2014, Obama sent troops back to Iraq after IS militants seized large swaths of territory, including Mosul. A coalition of more than 80 countries led by the US was formed to fight IS, which subjugated millions during a cruel war before losing its hold in Iraq in 2017 and in Syria in 2019.
In 2024, during Joe Biden’s presidency, the US and Iraq agreed to wind down the US-led coalition operations.

Some analysts fear that Iraqi security forces remain unprepared to ensure the country’s stability. Jassim al-Bahadli, who also serves as an adviser to the security forces, told Reuters that security vacuums can be extremely dangerous. Mohammed al-Juburi, a retired Iraqi army general, also told Reuters that the most important question is whether Iraq has prepared a plan for this new phase.

articles.title: No 10 gathering evidence on public support for rejoining the EU
articles.summary:
Senior Downing Street officials reach out to thinktanks and pollsters as they look to test backing for reversing Brexit

Senior Downing Street officials have been reaching out to thinktanks…

blocks.text: Senior Downing Street officials have been reaching out to thinktanks and pollsters as they look to test public support for the UK rejoining the EU.

Aides to Andy Burnham have been talking to EU experts in a range of organisations about how the public would view a promise to rejoin, as momentum builds behind including such a pledge in the next Labour manifesto.

Some in No 10 are keen to promise that Labour would at least negotiate over re-entry to the bloc, something Burnham has said he wanted to see happen “in his lifetime”. Others are nervous, however, that making such a promise could revive the flagging political fortunes of Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader.

Burnham used his first conference speech as the Labour leader to announce a review of the options for Britain’s relationship with Europe, and added on Wednesday that these options should include rejoining entirely.

The prime minister told delegates on Tuesday: “Brexit has done more harm than good. So I will take the opportunity around the [UK-EU] summit to lay out to you, to lay out to the country, what I believe are the different options for Britain’s long-term relationship with our European partners.”

blocks.caption: Andy Burnham announced a review of the options for Britain’s relationship with Europe in his speech at the Labour party conference. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian

blocks.text: On Wednesday he clarified that this would include an option to rejoin – something ruled out by his predecessor Keir Starmer.
Burnham told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “We could stay as we are. That’s definitely an option, if people think this is the right place to stay.

“We could look at what [the former Conservative chancellor] George Osborne has said about a customs union, we could look at what the Liberal Democrats said at their conference about the single market, or we could go all the way.”
Burnham’s comments sparked joy among pro-EU campaigners, who argue that rejoining is the best way to boost UK growth rates – and outrage from political opponents.
Alex Burghart, the Conservative deputy leader, said: “Labour cannot blame a democratic vote from over a decade ago for the consequences of their own economic decisions.”

The Guardian has learned, however, that Burnham’s comments are part of a wider effort by No 10 to test consensus over rejoining, with a view to possibly including such a promise in the next manifesto.
Officials have been in talks with several prominent thinktanks and pollsters who have been working on projects to flesh out arguments over rejoining and test public opinion.

Last week, the Tony Blair Institute released a paper arguing that Burnham should seek talks with Brussels over becoming a member once more, but only do so if Europe relaxed its regulations in sectors including energy and technology.

On the same day the pro-EU campaign group Best for Britain released a megapoll conducted by YouGov suggesting Labour could more than double its seat total if it went into the next election promising to rejoin.

Over the coming weeks, the influential Institute for Public Policy Research will also release a paper calling for the country to rejoin, while Think Labour has also been looking into how difficult it would be to do so.

Some in Downing Street are buoyed up by polling which shows that promising to re-enter the bloc does little to boost support for Reform. They also point out that Farage attacked the prime minister’s speech for the promise to change the pensions triple lock, rather than his comments about Europe.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Pro-EU campaigners argue that rejoining is the best way to boost UK growth rates. Photograph: Vuk Valcic/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The Guardian has been told that some at the top of government wanted the prime minister to use this week’s speech to promise to begin work on rejoining after the next election, rather than carrying out a review.

In the end, such an option was ruled out because the party was already bracing itself for a fight over pensions, and did not want to give succour to Farage while he faces accusations about millions of pounds’ worth of donations to his party.
No 10 said the prime minister did not ever consider making such a promise in the speech, and that it was not included in any draft of it.
Some believe it would be difficult to persuade Brussels, which has engaged in multiple rounds of talks about Britain’s relationship with the EU, to embark on negotiations over re-accession.

But in a major boost to supporters of rejoining, Emmanuel Macron on Wednesday welcomed Burnham’s comments. “Welcome back,” the French president said in English at a press conference in Madrid on Wednesday.
He continued in French: “If the British want to come back and if the prime minister is moving in that direction, I think that is very good news, both for his country and for the Europeans.”

An EU spokesperson said: “The UK is a close and valued partner of the European Union. It is for the UK government to set out how it wishes to develop its relationship with the EU going forward. We remain open to engaging on the options it may put forward.”

Burnham’s willingness to look at all options seems to have been accompanied by fresh engagement on the EU’s Made in Europe legislation, which threatens to lock UK goods out of certain supply chains on the continent.

No 10 has sought to have British manufacturers classified as European for the purposes of that legislation, with officials threatening to delay an EU-UK summit until London received signals that there could be an accommodation.
Since Burnham’s speech, however, there is now talk of holding a summit on 20 November.
One EU diplomat said it was necessary to get Starmer’s old reset agenda concluded before talks of “a real reset” could begin, confirming support for a UK-EU summit as early as possible.
A second diplomat said there was “a good feeling” that Burnham was now looking at all options and seeking a consensus, “something Brussels has wanted to see”.

articles.title: Arizona university hockey coach put on paid leave after report on Canadian NHL prospect's collapse
articles.summary: Arizona State University hockey coach Greg Powers has been placed on paid administrative leave after an anonymous letter from teammates of NHL prospect Matthew Mayich disputed aspects of the school's…

image.caption: Hamilton-born Matthew Mayich, who was drafted by the NHL's St. Louis Blues in 2023, was at an early-morning outdoor workout with the Arizona State University hockey team on Aug. 20 when he collapsed. (St. Louis Blues)

blocks.text: Hamilton·New

Arizona State University hockey coach Greg Powers has been placed on paid administrative leave after an anonymous letter from teammates of NHL prospect Matthew Mayich disputed aspects of the school's review into the Hamilton-born player's collapse during an outdoor workout last month.
Hamilton-born NHL prospect still in hospital after suffering issues during Aug. 20 outdoor workout

Arizona State University (ASU) hockey coach Greg Powers has been placed on paid administrative leave after a letter from teammates of NHL prospect Matthew Mayich disputed aspects of the school's review into the Canadian player's collapse during a team workout last month.

ASU athletics director Graham Rossini said in a news release Wednesday that "our focus continues to be on Matthew and his family and on our student athletes to make sure they have the support they need during this time and as the season begins.”

“We have continued to collect as much information as possible. After thorough and careful deliberation, I believe this is the best move to provide stability for the hockey program,” Rossini said about the coach being place on leave.

items: Matthew Mayich's Arizona teammates dispute school report on workout before Hamilton NHL prospect's collapse

blocks.text: In the review released last week, ASU official James Rund wrote that Hamilton-born Mayich, 21, collapsed just before 8:30 a.m. during Aug. 20 training at Sun Angel Stadium on ASU’s Tempe campus. It also determined school hockey coaches didn't submit a plan for review by trainers before the training session.
Mayich remains in hospital in critical condition.

items: Hockey coaches didn't submit training plan before Matthew Mayich collapsed in workout: Arizona university

blocks.text: ASU assistant hockey coach Mike Corbett will lead the team as the season opens this weekend and an interim head coach will be named soon, the release Wednesday said.
Hockey conference supports ASU's decision

ASU's move regarding Powers comes after seven members of the hockey team, in the anonymous letter sent to the university's president through their lawyer, called for the team's coaching staff to be placed on leave pending an independent investigation.

The players' letter alleges Mayich "received no water" during the outdoor workout on a hot day and said that, to "our knowledge, no one involved has been placed on leave, suspended or disciplined. The head coach who selected the instructor and scheduled the session continues to lead our program."
ASU is one of the 10 teams in the National Collegiate Hockey Conference (NCHC), a men's Division 1 conference in the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA).
The NCHC said in a statement that it supports ASU's decision to place Powers on leave while the circumstances surrounding Mayich's "trauma" are examined.
It said concerns raised by the student athletes "deserve to be heard and thoroughly reviewed. We will not prejudge the findings of that review."
The NCHC will stay in contact with ASU about the review and the steps being taken to protect and support student athletes, the statement said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Brittany Spencer is a multi-platform reporter and producer based in Hamilton. She's previously worked with CBC in Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick covering politics, health care and the justice system. She's a graduate of Toronto Metropolitan University's journalism program and joined CBC in 2017. You can reach her at brittany.spencer@cbc.ca.
