articles.title: ‘Strong indications’ that Iran played role in RAF Fairford incident, says Burnham
articles.summary:
PM also defends decision to release suspects on bail and expresses ‘complete confidence’ in security services

There are “strong indications” that Iran played a role in events in which five…

blocks.text: There are “strong indications” that Iran played a role in events in which five men were arrested near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire as part of a terror investigation, Andy Burnham has said.
Speaking to the media at the end of the Labour party conference in Liverpool, Burnham said he could not give any more details amid a police investigation, but that Iran was believed to be involved.

On Tuesday, Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, said Washington believed “a foreign actor” was involved in the events on Sunday night at the airbase, which has been used by US planes for missions against Iran.

In an interview with BBC News, Burnham said: “There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford, but of course it remains an ongoing, complex, and serious police investigation.
“And of course, we are working closely with our colleagues in the United States of America. So it’s ongoing.”
Noting that he had held a meeting of the government’s Cobra emergency committee while in Liverpool, Burnham said: “We are on top of it in every possible way imaginable.”
He added: “We will say more in due course, but we can confirm our belief that we believe Iran to have played a part.”
Asked why he believed this, Burnham replied: “Well I can’t go into all of those details, but obviously I wouldn’t say it lightly.”

In a separate interview with Sky News, Burnham was asked if he needed to recall parliament, which is in recess for the party conference season. He replied: “At this stage there is not an urgent need to do that, but should that arise, of course, I wouldn’t hesitate.”

The five men, all in their 20s and from London, were arrested in the Gloucestershire countryside near the airbase after a local woman driving home saw a series of vans and men in masks, and called police.

They were first arrested on explosives charges and then later for preparing acts of terrorism. All five were released on police bail on Monday after an examination of what was found in the vans, and searches of addresses linked to them across London.
On Tuesday the Guardian reported increasing confidence of an Iranian link to the weekend’s events.
The decision to release the men has prompted criticism from the Trump administration, with Rubio saying he was “disturbed” by it.
Questioned by the BBC about US criticism of the bail decision, Burnham said this had happened only with very strict conditions.

He said: “I think people need to understand that when it says released, that isn’t as people might think. It’s obviously with the strictest possible bail conditions. We’ve been talking to counterparts in the United States all week to explain what is happening here, how things are being done. I have complete confidence in the way British security services are handling this.”
It emerged on Tuesday that one of the five men arrested called the police to report the incident.
The local woman who also phoned police subsequently told newspapers that she was alarmed the men had been allowed to get so close to the airbase without apparently being noticed.
However, UK officials and Wes Streeting, the UK defence secretary, have indicated that security services were aware in advance of what was happening.
A statement from Britain’s head of counter-terrorism police hinted that officers swooped on the rural location for several reasons.

Assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor said: “A police response was activated in the early hours of Sunday morning due to a range of information received, including a call from a member of the public about several vehicles acting suspiciously close to RAF Fairford.”

articles.title: Fined telcos ask NTC for due process
articles.summary: The country’s biggest telcos are asking the National Telecommunications Commission (NTC) to observe due process after they were slapped with a daily fine of P100,000 over internet quality.

blocks.text: October 1, 2026 | 12:00am

In a statement, the Philippine Chamber of Telecommunication Operators (PCTO), made up of companies including PLDT Inc. and Globe Telecom Inc., demanded the NTC extend due process to telcos before handing out penalties.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — The country’s biggest telcos are asking the National Telecommunications Commission (NTC) to observe due process after they were slapped with a daily fine of P100,000 over internet quality.
The PCTO said the NTC has started charging fines over internet quality upon the issuance of show-cause orders.
The telcos were unable to air their side and contest the findings. Further, they questioned the process by which the NTC had arrived at the conclusion that their internet services are poor.

The PCTO said it recognizes the NTC’s memorandum circular requiring periodic audits on telco performance. However, the NTC has yet to outline the methodologies for the audit, from actual metrics to testing conditions.
“Operators should not be penalized under standards that have not been clearly defined and have not been consistently applied,” the PCTO said.
The telcos flagged the government for regulatory uncertainty and its penalty regime, as resources have to be diverted to paying fines instead of network investments.
They also attacked the NTC for failing to address longstanding issues on the local level, ranging from varying local government permitting to costly charges and lengthy approvals.
PLDT, Globe and Dito Telecommunity Corp. were imposed a P100,000 a day penalty until such time they have upgraded network assets to improve internet coverage in certain areas.
Globe was told to step up efforts in Makati and Quezon City; PLDT unit Smart Communications Inc. in Manila, Parañaque and Pasig and Dito, in Las Piñas, Pasay and San Juan.

articles.title: Bonoan remains accused in graft case
articles.summary: Former public works secretary Manuel Bonoan will remain as Sen. Jinggoy Estrada’s co-accused in a graft case linked to the flood control controversy.

blocks.text: October 1, 2026 | 12:00am
Former Public Works and Highways secretary Manuel Bonoan attends the Senate Blue Ribbon Committee hearing on the flood control controversy on Monday, January 19, 2026.
Senate PRIB / Released
MANILA, Philippines — Former public works secretary Manuel Bonoan will remain as Sen. Jinggoy Estrada’s co-accused in a graft case linked to the flood control controversy.
The Sandiganbayan Second Division has affirmed its ruling denying prosecutors’ bid to drop Bonoan as a defendant.
Bonoan is accused of conspiring with Estrada to ensure that flood control projects in Bulacan were included in the 2025 national budget.
Estrada allegedly received P213.7 million in kickbacks.
In a separate plunder case involving Estrada, the Sandiganbayan Fifth Division had dropped Bonoan as co-accused and released him from detention.
Bonoan is out on bail.
The ombudsman earlier asked the courts to drop the charges against Bonoan so he could be considered a state witness.

During pre-trial, Estrada’s lawyers said they will mark as evidence former Bulacan district engineer Brice Hernandez’s affidavit, which stated that Estrada lacked participation in the alleged kickback scheme.
Brice pleads not guilty
Hernandez and six others have pleaded not guilty to graft charges involving an alleged P77-million ghost flood control project in Balagtas, Bulacan.

Before the anti-graft court’s Fifth Division, Hernandez and former public works officials Jaypee Mendoza, Arjay Domaig, Niño Morales, Juanito Mendoza, Floralyn Simbulan and Christina Pineda entered their not-guilty pleas.
Three others were not arraigned since they are still at large, namely former lawmaker and fugitive Zaldy Co and his staff members John Paul Estrada and Mark Tecsay.
The P77-million flood control project was declared 100 percent complete by May 2025 even though it only started in February 2025.
The structure did not exist, according to the Office of the Ombudsman.
Rep. Rivera suspended
Tarlac Rep. Noel Rivera has been suspended for 90 days over alleged conflict of interest in government infrastructure projects.

Facing two graft cases, Rivera is accused of maintaining financial interests in nine infrastructure projects awarded to Tarlac 3-G Construction and Development Corp. during his term as lawmaker from 2022 to 2025.
Rivera is one of the alleged “cong-tractors” involved in the flood control scam.
Rivera allegedly owned a controlling stake in the firm, which won a P94.86-million contract in 2023 for a road project in San Narcisco, Zambales.

articles.title: Palace tells Velasco to face probe; houses raided
articles.summary: Malacañang has advised former House speaker Lord Allan Velasco to come forward and shed light on the allegations against him after the Bureau of Immigration (BI) confirmed that he left the…

blocks.text: October 1, 2026 | 12:00am

Image shows dismissed police officer Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. (center) with former speaker Lord Allan Velasco and Vice President Sara Duterte. This is one of the photographs included with the affidavit Gracioso submitted to the NBI.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — Malacañang has advised former House speaker Lord Allan Velasco to come forward and shed light on the allegations against him after the Bureau of Immigration (BI) confirmed that he left the country on Aug. 30 and did not come home on his expected date of return.?

Velasco may clear the air after dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr., the lawmaker’s former security officer, claimed in an affidavit that he delivered more than P2 billion in cash to Vice President Sara Duterte and members of her family, including her father, former president Rodrigo Duterte.
The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) is now probing the claims of Gracioso, who alleged that the cash deliveries, in suitcases, were made upon Velasco’s orders.

Velasco’s camp has denied the allegations, saying Gracioso’s “one-size-fits-all narration” appears to be “designed and fabricated to attack as many targets as it can while being inconsistent with verifiable events.”?
The BI said Velasco flew to Japan on Aug. 30 and did not return to Manila on Sept. 14, his date of arrival.

“Whether he is afraid or is just taking a vacation, we cannot tell. But if his name is mentioned in the millions contained in suitcases allegedly delivered to the Vice President, (former) president Duterte and Congressman Pulong Duterte, it would be better if he sheds light on it so he can clear his name and that of his wife,” Palace press officer Claire Castro said at a media briefing yesterday.
The NBI intends to invite people named in Gracioso’s affidavit, including Velasco’s wife, Rowena, who reportedly left the country on Sept. 24.
Gracioso yesterday underwent a lie detector test at the NBI. Results have not been published yet.
In a 1978 decision, the Supreme Court said it “does not put much faith and credit on” a lie detector test.
NBI raids houses
NBI agents with a search warrant raided houses allegedly owned by Velasco in Valle Verde, Pasig on Aug. 24, according to NBI Director Melvin Matibag.
Matibag told reporters on Tuesday that operatives initially didn’t know that the properties belonged to Velasco because they were registered under the names of his employees and a certain company.
Operatives seized firearms, bullets, magazines and IDs belonging to police and security personnel.
Former lawmaker Mikee Romero claimed in a Facebook post on Sept. 25 that Velasco’s home was being raided “now” by the NBI.
However, it was unclear whether it was a separate raid that Romero referred to or the same one that Matibag had confirmed. – EJ Macababbad

articles.title: Digital platform launched for anti-dynasty law initiative
articles.summary: The People’s Initiative Coalition Against Dynasty, through its Dapat Isa Lang initiative, launched a digital signature platform yesterday in its push to end political dynasties.

blocks.text: October 1, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The People’s Initiative Coalition Against Dynasty (PICAD), through its Dapat Isa Lang initiative, launched a digital signature platform yesterday in its push to end political dynasties.
PICAD convenor Eirene Aguila said the initiative aims to collect 7.5 million signatures, with 10 percent coming from registered voters nationwide and the other three percent from each district.
She said the digital platform is “a vehicle to exercise constitutional power” and is not a form of rebellion but “democracy in the most peaceful form.”
“In a people’s initiative, we’re not just mere voters. We help in shaping the law,” she said.
Dapat Isa Lang initially used to collect signatures manually, but it was halted when the coalition decided to move it to a digital platform to be more inclusive.
“The goal is inclusivity. We want everyone’s participation in this campaign,” Karlo Abadines, head of Dapat Isa Lang stated.
When asked about the accessibility, he said they already talked to their partners to organize digital kiosks.
“You can invite community members to go to our partner schools, churches. Our personnel will help them and will provide devices for them to sign the petition,” Abadines said.
PICAD chairman Antonio Carpio demonstrated the step-by-step process on how to sign the petition online through d1l.org.
According to him, the entire process may only last three minutes.

Speaking at the launch of the digital signature platform, former Commission on Elections (Comelec) chairman and member of the 1986 Constitutional Commission Christian Monsod said gathering 7.3 million signatures in four months is “a huge, huge task.”
“We will help you in this task because we know it’s a difficult one,” he declared.
During his speech, Monsod admitted he initially proposed that the ban on political dynasties should no longer be included in the current Charter but he later withdrew it.

“During the deliberations by the Constitutional Commission on this issue, I myself said ‘wait, if you have this prohibition on dynasties, maybe there are those who are good and honest who happen to belong to a political family and we’re saying he cannot run because of this anti-dynasty provision,’” he said.
While on recess, he said he realized the need to retain the anti-political dynasty provision after discussions with fellow members of the commission.
For instance, such a ban was a “cost and benefit issue” and that it would “open the door to the millions of poor Filipinos who deserve to be in public office,” he said.

Also, the ban on political dynasties would “close the door on the circumvention of the term limits,” especially with succession of family members in elective positions, and at the same time promote “equitable distribution of power for the common good.”
Eventually, Monsod said he “withdrew” his proposal to exclude the political dynasty ban.
Suspension lifted
The Comelec has lifted its suspension on the rules governing people’s initiative for legislative amendments, Chairman George Garcia said on Tuesday.

Speaking at the Kapihan sa Manila Bay forum, he said the Comelec had previously suspended its rules covering both constitutional and legislative amendments, but later lifted the suspension on legislative matters following discussions with Congress.
Garcia said the move means there is no longer a procedural barrier for groups seeking to use a people’s initiative to push for legislation, including a proposed ban on political dynasties.
However, Garcia noted that the Comelec still has to address the use of electronic signatures, which are not currently covered by its existing rules on people’s initiative.
Meanwhile, the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) reminded barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan officials that the extension of their term is not an exemption from liabilities.
The DILG said longer term means greater responsibility and accountability, and officials should not take advantage of their extended tenure.

The department said it would continue guiding and provide technical assistance to barangay and SK officials to ensure they remain responsive to their constituents’ needs. – Ghio Ong, Christine Boton, Emmanuel Tupas

articles.title: OP, others given 5 days to answer BSKE deferment plea
articles.summary: The Supreme Court has directed the Office of the President, the Commission on Elections and both chambers of Congress to comment within five days on the petition against the postponement of the…

blocks.text: October 1, 2026 | 12:00am
A legal challenge to the postponement of the Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE) is filed with the Supreme Court in Manila on September 28, 2026.
Edd Gumban / The Philippine STAR

MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court (SC) has directed the Office of the President, the Commission on Elections and both chambers of Congress to comment within five days on the petition against the postponement of the barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan elections (BSKE) to November 2028.

The SC’s order stemmed from a petition for certiorari and prohibition filed by election lawyer Romulo Macalintal contesting the implementation of Republic Act 12326 postponing the elections. RA 12326 was signed by President Marcos on Sept. 24 and became immediately executory.
The SC gave the respondents “a non-extendible period of five calendar days from notice” to submit their comments.
Macalintal said he was “deeply glad and thankful that the SC immediately acted on our petition.”
The development, he added, was “a clear indication that the High Court sees substantial merits in our petition.”
In his petition, Macalintal wants the SC to issue a temporary restraining order or status quo ante order on RA 12326.
The law signed by Marcos also fixed the term of BSK officials to five years from the current four, with two terms for barangay officials and one term for SK officials.
Macalintal earlier said RA 12326 “violates the electorate’s right to vote by postponing the 2026 BSKE under the guise of fixing the officials’ term of office.”

He said the postponement was “unduly long” starting with the rescheduling of the December 2025 BSKE to November this year, and another postponement to November 2028, or a total of three years of extension.
He said the Comelec should continue with its preparations for BSKE, originally scheduled in November, as the high court might rule in his favor.
He also cited a favorable SC ruling on his petition questioning the postponement of the BSKE in December 2022 through RA 11935.
Macalintal said the SC’s decision then to declare RA 11935 unconstitutional was a “very clear precedent.”

articles.title: Marcos Jr. institutionalizes online budget monitoring portal
articles.summary: Amid corruption scandals, Filipinos may soon be able to track online how their hard-earned taxes are spent as President Marcos issued an executive order institutionalizing an online portal designed…

blocks.text: October 1, 2026 | 12:00am

The Centralized Open Monitoring Platform for Appropriations and Spending Statistics (COMPASS) portal will help the public monitor expenditures, procurement and implementation of state projects by making information about such activities more accessible.
Philstar.com / Irish Lising

MANILA, Philippines — Amid corruption scandals, Filipinos may soon be able to track online how their hard-earned taxes are spent as President Marcos issued an executive order institutionalizing an online portal designed to promote transparency in the use of state funds.

Described by the budget department as the country’s first centralized digital platform for monitoring government appropriations and spending, COMPASS may use distributed ledger technology, including blockchain and other emerging technologies, to perform its purpose.

“The portal shall promote transparency, accountability, and public participation by providing timely, reliable, and user-friendly access to government financial and performance information across the budget cycle,” Marcos’ Executive Order 126 dated Sept. 28 read.
Marcos ordered agencies to use COMPASS as his administration continues to grapple with corruption issues particularly involving flood control projects.
The Philippine economy may have lost some P118.5 billion every year from 2023 to 2025 to corruption in flood control projects, according to the finance department’s estimates.

The EO required national government agencies and instrumentalities to submit, regularly update, disclose and publish relevant information through COMPASS. It also encouraged local governments to use the platform.

“Transparency and accountability should not be complicated. The Filipino people have the right to know how their money is being used, and whether that spending is delivering results,” Executive Secretary Ralph Recto said in a statement yesterday.
“Every peso comes from the people. They should be able to see where it goes, what it pays for, and what government delivers in return,” he added.

The portal, launched by the budget department in June, may be linked with government financial, procurement, monitoring and digital systems like the Integrated Financial Management Information System, the Budget and Treasury Management System, the Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System, the Digital Information for Monitoring and Evaluation, and the E-Gov PH App.

The portal will also provide information about projects funded through public-private partnerships and foreign-assisted programs insofar as they involve public funds coursed through national government agencies or other relevant government mechanisms. It will not cover information that cannot be disclosed publicly under existing laws, including those that could compromise national defense and security or violate the Data Privacy Act.

A COMPASS Council will provide policy direction and strategic oversight for the implementation of the platform. The budget department will chair the council with the information and communications technology department as co-chair. Designated as members are the finance and interior departments.

Meanwhile, the Office of the President’s P10.1-billion proposed budget breezed through the Senate finance committee yesterday, with no lawmaker raising questions on the nearly P4.5-billion allocation for confidential and intelligence funds (CIF). It underwent only 16 minutes of deliberations by the committee. - Neil Jayson Servallos

articles.title: PLDT wants to block violent ‘grooming’ sites
articles.summary: Telco giant PLDT Inc. is appealing to the government to grant providers the power to unilaterally block sites without regulatory approval, to improve online safety and prevent copycat effects.

blocks.text: October 1, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Telco giant PLDT Inc. is appealing to the government to grant providers the power to unilaterally block sites without regulatory approval, to improve online safety and prevent copycat effects.
On the sidelines of an online child safety forum, PLDT chief operating officer Menardo Jimenez Jr. backed legislation empowering telcos to block violent sites.

Jimenez cited Republic Act 11930, which requires internet service providers to detect and block sites promoting online sexual abuse and exploitation of children and to report such activity to the Philippine National Police within 24 hours.
He pointed out that PLDT has detected channels promoting violence or nihilistic violent extremism but has yet to secure regulatory approval to block them.

“I think if we are given the right guidelines, either by the law or by the right government entity, I would prefer some level of empowerment. If we are able to see and confirm that there are certain sites that actually do violent acts, [I hope we are empowered] to shut them down,” Jimenez said.
Such authority could also encourage telcos to compete to become the provider with the safest network for children, according to Jimenez.
Stricter child-safety policy

The issue of online safety also figured in the Senate as Akbayan Youth on Wednesday opposed a proposed outright ban on social media use by people below 18, urging lawmakers to consider stricter child-safety measures instead.
Akbayan Youth national chairperson Khylla Meneses argued that restricting access alone would not necessarily protect young people online.
“We cannot protect young people simply by closing the door. We need to make the digital spaces they enter safer,” Meneses said in Filipino.
The group cautioned that an outright ban could drive young users to less regulated online spaces, where parents and authorities may have fewer safeguards and oversight mechanisms.

Instead, Akbayan proposed prohibiting social media accounts for children aged 13 and below while strengthening privacy protections, age-assurance systems, parental controls and accountability measures for social media platforms.
“Social media companies should be accountable for dangerous design, harmful content and inadequate safeguards,” the group said.

The position came as the Senate considers Senate Bill 2066, which seeks to establish a minimum age for social media use, regulate children’s access to social media platforms and impose obligations on social media providers.
Introduced by Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian, the bill was referred to the Senate committees on public information and mass media, and science and technology.

The move is in line with President Marcos’ vow to carry out measures to ensure the safety of students in the face of growing concerns over three recent school shootings that have left a total of nine persons dead.
More work remains

In his remarks during the celebration of National Teachers’ Month in Manila, Marcos yesterday said the government has done much to change the course of Philippine education, but acknowledged that “much work still remains.”

He cited the need to remedy the gaps in how teachers are prepared and developed, including the assigning of educators to subjects outside their specialization and provide a safe environment for learners.

“Teachers do more than just teach lessons. For many of our children, they become second parents in school, helping create environments where learners feel safe, supported and cared for,” Marcos said. “This also means strengthening school safety and student support. Together with parents, communities and other partners, we will continue to work to make our schools more secure and more responsive to the needs of our learners.”
The discussions followed a series of school shooting scares, including an incident at Isulan National High School in Sultan Kudarat.
Yesterday, a loud sound initially perceived as gunfire caused panic among students and teachers, prompting an investigation and the suspension of face-to-face classes.
Sultan Kudarat Gov. Datu Pax Ali Mangudadatu later revealed that there was no shooting and that the sound was likely caused by faulty electrical wiring.
No ammunition was found at the site, he said, while the Bureau of Fire Protection continued its investigation.
The DepEd Division Office of Sultan Kudarat assured the public that the situation was under control with no reported injuries or casualties.
The loud sound caused widespread panic on campus, with students seen in viral videos posted on Facebook securing themselves inside classrooms amid fears of an active shooter.
Police and military officials said the incident also caused alarm among parents after reports of a supposed shooting circulated on social media.
As a precautionary measure, the local government of Isulan suspended face-to-face classes Wednesday afternoon until further notice.
“We urge everyone to remain calm and refrain from sharing unverified information,” the DepEd division office said.

The incident came amid heightened concern over threats against schools in Region 12 following a deadly shooting at Banga National High School in South Cotabato on Sept. 18 that left three people dead and six others wounded.

South Cotabato Gov. Reynaldo Tamayo Jr. said Wednesday that psychologists and social welfare personnel are counseling 40 students who were apprehended for making online threats to attack schools in separate operations in South Cotabato and Sultan Kudarat over the past 10 days.
Twenty of the students are from different towns in South Cotabato while another 20 are from different towns in Sultan Kudarat.
Tamayo said the students, who include elementary and high school students, are being treated as children needing psychological interventions rather than law offenders.
Counselors from units of the Police Regional Office 12 are also helping rehabilitate the students.

Meanwhile, Baguio City police are investigating messages circulated among students of the Philippine Science High School-Cordillera Administrative Region Campus in Barangay Irisan that were perceived as threats.
Personnel of Baguio City Police Station 9 launched an inquiry on Sept. 29 following a Facebook post alleging threatening messages linked to the school.
According to a police report, school officials told investigators that the claims stemmed from an earlier incident and a reported group chat containing statements involving a firearm.
Authorities have yet to establish any confirmed threat or attack plan.

No firearm has also been reported recovered and police have made no criminal finding arising from the inquiry. – Evelyn Macairan, Emmanuel Tupas, Roel Pareño, Art Dumlao, John Unson, Mark Ernest Villeza, Alexis Romero

articles.title: SC junks petitions vs lower impeach vote to convict
articles.summary: The Supreme Court has junked the three petitions challenging the ruling of the Senate impeachment court that allowed a lower number of votes to convict Vice President Sara Duterte.

blocks.text: October 1, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court has junked the three petitions challenging the ruling of the Senate impeachment court that allowed a lower number of votes to convict Vice President Sara Duterte.

The Supreme Court dismissed the three separate petitions filed by former executive secretary Vic Rodriguez, lawyer Ernesto Francisco Jr. and disbarred lawyer Berteni Causing, according to the SC’s press briefer issued yesterday.
Their petitions were shelved due to “lack of standing and prematurity,” the SC noted.
The impeachment court welcomed the dismissal of the petitions, declaring that it rendered the trial “constitutionally bulletproof.”

“By junking these challenges, the highest court has drawn a definitive firewall around the independence of the Senate as an impeachment court, confirming that its proceedings cannot be held hostage by premature judicial meddling or collateral litigation,” impeachment court spokesman Reginald Tongol said.

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said the SC’s refusal to issue a temporary restraining order and status quo ante order validates the chamber’s actions allowing a variable vote denominator to convict.
“It means that what the impeachment court is doing is within its bounds and within its constitutional allowance,” Gatchalian said.
The House prosecution also welcomed the SC ruling.

“It allows the trial to proceed without delay and keeps the focus where it belongs – on the evidence already before the Senate impeachment court,” panel spokesman Lanao del Sur Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong said.
House prosecutor Bicol Saro Party-list Rep. Terry Ridon said the SC ruling would allow the impeachment proceedings to continue without further distraction.

The two-thirds threshold would hinge on the number of senator-judges actually present during the impeachment trial, which now stands at 20 from the regular 24 due to various reasons. This would make the new threshold to convict respondent at 14.

At present, Sens. Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta are detained due to their plunder and graft cases while Sen. Ronald dela Rosa, who is subject of an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court, remains at large. Sen. Loren Legarda has been overseas and on medical leave since August.

Last week, the impeachment court ruled the constitutional provision requiring “two-thirds of all members of the Senate” to convict impeachable officials excluded in particular senators who are detained and suspended, in hiding or on sick leave.
Bank records

The House prosecution panel may begin presenting the subpoenaed bank records of Vice President Duterte today as the Senate impeachment court shifts to full-day hearings on her alleged unexplained wealth.
House prosecution spokesman Ace Barbers said they are ready to go deeper into the financial evidence under Article II of the Vice President’s impeachment trial.
“This will be a fruitful week because we might start presenting the bank records today and tomorrow,” he said.
Prosecutors intend to compare Duterte’s declared wealth and lawful sources of income with financial transactions reflected in records obtained from banks and other institutions.

The impeachment court earlier authorized subpoenas for peso-denominated bank records involving Duterte, her husband Manases Carpio and several entities after finding the requested documents prima facie relevant and material to Article II.
The prosecution said more than 1,800 bank, insurance and other financial documents have since been subjected to marking and processing ahead of their presentation in court.

The panel has offered to enter into stipulations with the defense on the subpoenaed bank records in an effort to dispense with as many as 20 bank representatives who would otherwise have to testify to authenticate the documents.
Barbers said the impeachment court has allotted longer hearing hours this week to accelerate the presentation of evidence.
“Yes, full day, from 10 a.m. Thursday with no time limit. It will be the same on Friday,” he said.
Dangerous precedent

Davao City Mayor Sebastian Duterte’s claim that he was not aware he was transacting with a firm connected to his sister, the Vice President, sets a “dangerous” precedent for other local executives, Malacañang said yesterday.

Palace press officer Claire Castro said the doctrine established by the ruling on Arias v Sandiganbayan may be invoked but not frequently, to cover up for one’s weakness or the anomalies of an ally or a sibling. The SC said the Arias doctrine states that all heads of offices have to rely to a reasonable extent on their subordinates and on the good faith of those who prepare bids, purchase supplies or enter into negotiations.
There has to be some added reason why the head of office should examine each of the documents he is supposed to sign, the high court said.

“We are just basing it on what we heard and what he (Sebastian) knows and what he mentioned in the hearing yesterday (Sept. 29), on how long he has been a mayor and how come he does not look at the contracts he is signing,” Castro said.
“It will be dangerous if used by other mayors to claim that they do not know that they are transacting with a sibling,” she added.
Thrown under the bus?

Castro clarified that she is not passing judgment on the mayor, who claimed during his testimony as a hostile witness on Tuesday that he was not aware of the Vice President’s connection to GenCorp Industries Inc.
The Davao City government awarded 19 contracts to GenCorp.

“He (Sebastian) showed that he did not know anything and it seemed that he did not care. But when Sen. (Panfilo) Lacson mentioned the Arias v Sandiganbayan, it seemed that he defended himself as a mayor,” Castro said.

“He (Sebastian) lifted himself as a mayor, but in a way, he threw his sister under the bus when he said that had he known that (she) had interest in GenCorp, he would not have allowed it. But this is not a judgment. We are just basing it on what he heard from his narrative. But still, again, we should not judge Mayor Baste Duterte based on his own statements.” – Alexis Romero, Neil Jayson Servallos

articles.title: French court jails six men for manslaughter over mass drowning in Channel
articles.summary:
Seven others found guilty of lesser charges in connection to incident in 2021 when inflatable dinghy sank killing at least 27 people with four more missing, presumed dead

A Paris court has…

blocks.text: A Paris court has jailed six ⁠men for manslaughter over the deaths of at least 27 people in the worst mass drowning on record from a small-boat crossing in the Channel.
Seven other men were ⁠found guilty of lesser smuggling charges with varying degrees of seriousness, including facilitating illegal immigration as part of ⁠an organised gang and criminal conspiracy.
Five years on, another four people are still missing.
The court heard that the sinking of an inflatable dinghy in November 2021 was caused by “individuals driven by greed, with utter disregard for human life”.
Prosecutors said the convicted men helped launch a “substandard small boat, uncertified, unfit for navigation on the open sea, overcrowded and lacking appropriate lifejackets”.
Emmanuel Daoud, a lawyer for one victim’s family, called the proceedings a “trial of greed, cynicism and inhumanity”.
Twenty-seven people were confirmed dead when their inflatable dinghy sank in the early hours of 24 November 2021. Four people remain unaccounted for.

blocks.caption: Lawyers and relatives of victims arrive at court in Paris for the trial of the alleged smugglers. Photograph: Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The victims were mostly Iraqi Kurds, but also included people who were Afghan, Ethiopian, Iranian, Somali, Vietnamese and Egyptian. The youngest known victim was a seven-year-old girl. The confirmed dead included 15 men, seven women and two teenagers.

Sentences for the six men found guilty of manslaughter ranged ‌from six to 10 years in prison. For others, sentences ranged from six months suspended to four ​years in prison. The court heard that the men were linked to Afghan and Iraqi-Kurdish smuggling networks ⁠that organised the migrants’ passage to Britain from camps near Grande-Synthe and Calais in northern France. One man was found innocent.

According to testimony from the two survivors, the flimsy boat, which had attempted to cross one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes between the northern French coast and Kent in southern England began to deflate and take on water after several hours at sea.
Passengers fell overboard and drowned one after another, despite making about a dozen desperate calls for help to French and British rescue services. Only two men survived.
For the people onboard the sinking boat, despite several distress calls, it was nearly 12 hours after the first pleas for help before the dinghy was finally found by a French fishing vessel.

A separate investigation is continuing in France into seven French military personnel – five members at a maritime rescue coordination centre, and two sailors onboard a patrol vessel. They have been under investigation since 2023 for failing to help a person in danger. They deny the allegations.
Zana Mahmand Mohammed travelled from Erbil in Iraqi Kurdistan to address the court about his younger brother, Twana, 18, who drowned in the disaster but whose body has never been found.

He said: “We’ve been waiting for our brother’s body for five years. I live with the uncertainty of ever finding out what happened. We lost a member of our family. He had a project for another future to live … ”

The family had tried to dissuade Twana from leaving home, but he had wanted to find a job and develop his sporting success as a black belt in taekwondo and escape the violence and insecurity of his region.
Mohammed said every time he read in the media about other small boats in difficulty, he relived the tragedy. “Destruction is being repeated,” he said.

articles.title: ‘We want justice’: series of rapes trigger mass protests at Indian universities
articles.summary:
Women say nothing has changed since Delhi’s infamous Nirbhaya bus rape case 14 years ago

The posters, just like the women holding them, were taking no prisoners. “Girls don’t need curfews,…
articles.byline: Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Aakash Hassan in Delhi

blocks.text: The posters, just like the women holding them, were taking no prisoners. “Girls don’t need curfews, rapists need consequences,” read one. “Lock your dicks rather than your women at home,” read another.

As hundreds of women walked from the gates of their university campus into the streets of Delhi – where sexual harassment, assault, catcalling and molestation are a constant, daily threat – they shouted together in a chorus of rage and defiance: “We want justice.”

The fury that has erupted on India’s university campuses over the past week has been double-edged. The trigger was a series of brutal rapes that have taken place in Delhi in recent weeks, including the alleged gang-rape of a 17-year-old in a public park close to Delhi University by three men who posed as police officers.

Just a week earlier, another 17-year-old was gang-raped and murdered in Delhi’s Swaroop Nagar neighbourhood after she went to meet friends. The accused allegedly raped her, stabbed her to death and dumped her body in a field, where it was discovered days later half eaten by dogs.
Rapes of an 11-year-old and a six-year-old were reported in the same month. Last month, a 16-year-old was allegedly raped by a bus driver and conductor after she boarded a sleeper bus in Delhi.

Women who have taken part in protests on Delhi university campuses have condemned these alleged violent rapes on minors as disgusting and unforgivable – but they have also been at pains to emphasise that they are not out of the ordinary.

Fourteen years have passed since Delhi’s infamous Nirbhaya rape case, when a woman was gang-raped on a bus and died from her injuries. But while it provoked international outrage and a slew of legislation and government promises, women say nothing has changed; for them, India’s streets, particularly in Delhi, remain as unsafe as ever. According to statistics, a women is raped in India every 20 minutes – though the real scale is believed to be far worse due to chronic under-reporting.
This week, the supreme court said the five successive rape cases “starkly underlined a systematic failure” and it could not help but “draw painful parallels to the Nirbhaya incident of 2012”.

Vaishnavi Dhruw, 21, a history student at Delhi University, was among the female protesters at the “smash the patriarchy” protest march on Wednesday afternoon. “I don’t know a single woman who lives in this city and feels safe,” she said.

blocks.caption: Students’ Federation of India (SFI) members protest over the alleged rape of a 17-year-old girl. Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPA

blocks.text: While some of the key demands of the protest have been better lighting and policing, Dhruw emphasised that for anything to change, the country required a deep societal shift where men no longer felt they had ownership over women’s bodies.

“We are not marching for safety, we are here to protest for our freedom, for the most basic right to walk in our own streets,” she said. “Again and again, women are told to stay indoors, to not go out at night, to cover ourselves, to protect ourselves. When will society tell men in our country not to rape?”

Much of the anger driving the protests has also been prompted by the response by the authorities to the rapes, which women say once again has only been to police their freedoms. Women in Delhi were told to stay out of parks at night, and classes were temporarily halted at one of Delhi’s most prestigious female colleges. Many hostels where female students stay impose strict curfews preventing them from going out at night.

“Instead of going after criminals, you’re going to tell women to sit at home,” said Aranya Rathore, 25, a student at Delhi University. “A demand for more surveillance is not a solution. In fact, it’s going to curtail our freedom more.”

Female students say a lot of their time is taken up by safety logistics – from wearing modest clothes to reorganising their days to ensure they do not travel alone or at night and always having a trackable live location on their phones. There is widespread awareness that should anything happen, the onus of blame – both within the family home and more widely in society – tends to fall on women. As one poster at Wednesday’s march pointed out, “no one ever asks what the rapist was wearing”.

Yet despite their best efforts, many women said it was almost impossible to avoid harassment. Ananya Wig, a 26-year-old graduate of Delhi University and the founder of Her Huq, a gender equality initiative, said she had experienced harassment both around university campuses and in public spaces.

She recounted an incident where a driver rolled down his car window and began masturbating as she and female friends got off a rickshaw and walked through the college gates. “This wasn’t at night, it was in the middle of the day,” she said. “I’ve always lived in Delhi and the city has not changed.”

The protests have brought into focus a dilemma faced by many Indian women, who are being educated in greater numbers than any time in the country’s history and have better job opportunities than ever before, but still have to navigate the constant debilitating threats to their safety and the conservative pressures from their families.

“I know so many girls, not just 10 years ago but even today, who end up choosing educational institutions and jobs and other employment opportunities depending on how close they are from their home,” said Wig. “Not on the basis of their marks, not on the basis of their aspirations, but simply, ‘OK, the shorter the distance is, the more likely it is that I will be safe’.”

Many of the Delhi University students who took part in the marches said that sexual harassment had become prevalent on campus, and have demanded better accountability mechanisms for reporting assault. The university has not responded.

Devyani Sarkar, 24, who is studying for a master’s in English, said: “Delhi University is one of the most prestigious universities in India right now but there are various cases of women being assaulted by professors, sometimes unfortunately also for grades. It’s despicable, but it’s also a living truth.”

Many on the marches said it was no coincidence that they were taking place in the aftermath of India’s “cockroach” movement, in which hundreds of thousands of young Gen Z Indians took to the streets over education reform.
“My generation is not afraid to stand up and protest. We know that society has to change,” said 17-year-old Subhani. “The days of women being silent is over.”

articles.title: Marcos extends Dizon, Lopez appointments
articles.summary: President Marcos has extended the appointments of acting Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon and acting Transportation Secretary Giovanni Lopez after their legal mandates expired, Executive Secretary…

blocks.text: September 30, 2026 | 11:41pm

MANILA, Philippines — President Marcos has extended the appointments of acting Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon and acting Transportation Secretary Giovanni Lopez after their legal mandates expired, Executive Secretary Ralph Recto confirmed yesterday.

Speaking to reporters following the Office of the President’s budget hearing at the Senate, Recto addressed the lapsed appointments of Dizon and Lopez, both of whom have yet to face the Commission on Appointments (CA) since assuming their posts last year.
Recto said all secretaries would be submitted for confirmation hearings before the bicameral CA “at the appropriate time.”
“We will get there, but for now the President extended the appointment of these two Cabinet members,” he added.

The announcement came after a tense Senate budget deliberation last week, when President Marcos’ sister, Sen. Imee Marcos, confronted Dizon over his legal authority to continue leading the Department of Public Works and Highways.
Citing the Administrative Code of 1987, the senator pointed out that temporary designations cannot exceed one year. She noted that Dizon’s appointment from September last year had lapsed by 24 days.

articles.title: Philippines falls in innovation index
articles.summary: The Philippines slipped two places in the 2026 Global Innovation Index, as limited resources for innovation outweigh the country’s growing capacity to produce high-tech outputs.

blocks.text: September 30, 2026 | 11:41pm

The Philippines ranked 52nd in this year’s index, released annually by the World Intellectual Property Organization, down from 50th in 2025. The country’s rank is bolstered by high-tech manufacturing and trade, but trailed in domestic invention capabilities.
STAR / File
MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines slipped two places in the 2026 Global Innovation Index, as limited resources for innovation outweigh the country’s growing capacity to produce high-tech outputs.
Despite the drop, the Philippines remains one of the world’s innovation over-performers along with China (10th), India (38th), Vietnam (43rd), Turkey (45th), Morocco (54th) and Indonesia (55th).
Manila ranked 49th in output rank, which measures tangible results from innovation activities.
It scored higher than the previous year in high-tech manufacturing, high-tech exports and information and communications technology services exports.
The Philippines and other middle-income economies struggle to foster a strong innovation environment and provide the necessary resources, the report said. – Louella Desiderio

articles.title: Sweden must apologise for harm done to Sami people, says state-backed report
articles.summary:
Independent commission accuses country of failing Indigenous people, amid rising tensions over land rights

An independent commission set up by the Swedish state has called on the country’s…

blocks.text: An independent commission set up by the Swedish state has called on the country’s government to apologise for the “harm and injustice inflicted upon the Sami people” and to start a national process for “redress and reconciliation”.

The Truth Commission for the Sami People also called for a special apology to be issued urgently to elderly Sami people who were forced as children to attend segregated so-called “nomad school” and other boarding schools where they were “subjected to violations or abuse”.

The commission’s report, published on Wednesday, is the outcome of a four-year investigation and hundreds of interviews with Sami people across Sweden. It was due to be presented to a government representative at a ceremony featuring readings from the text, but with no government yet in place after the election earlier this month, it went instead to Parisa Liljestrand, the last government’s culture minister.

The commission’s chair, Lena Nyberg, told her: “We hand over a big responsibility.” Liljestrand thanked the members of the commission and those who were interviewed for the report, saying it had been a “historic process”.

There have been similar truth commissions into the treatment of Sami people – Europe’s only recognised Indigenous people – in Norway and Finland. Norway has issued an official apology and discussions in Finland are ongoing.

The new report accuses Sweden of failing to meet its domestic and international human rights obligations and says that as a “direct consequence” of mistreatment, the Sami people today face “major challenges” in preserving and developing their culture.

blocks.caption: Plans to expand mining operations in Kiruna, Sweden, threaten traditional grazing lands used by Sami reindeer herders. Photograph: Johan Ylitalo/The Guardian

blocks.text: It coincides with rising anti-Sami rhetoric in Sweden, including from political leaders, amid clashes over land used for grazing by Sami reindeer herders for hundreds of years, which the state wants to mine for rare-earth minerals.

The report says issues with the handling of Sami land rights in Sweden have been “reinforced and aggravated” by an ideology that Sami people are “an inferior people and therefore neither deserving of nor capable of exercising the same rights and responsibilities as other citizens”.
It adds that the Swedish state has failed to implement the United Nations declaration on the rights of Indigenous peoples.

The commission’s 71-point call to action recommends an official apology for the harm and injustice inflicted upon the Sami people, as well as financial compensation and completing the process of ratifying the International Labour Organization’s convention on Indigenous and tribal peoples.
after newsletter promotion

It calls for the establishment of a national centre for redress and reconciliation, and for authorities to recognise that the Swedish nation was founded on lands belonging to two peoples – the Sámi and the Swedes – and that parts of the land have Sami names and are part of Sami cultural heritage.

It also urges recognition that Sápmi, the region traditionally inhabited by the Sami people, extends across present national borders; an end to racial discrimination against Sami people; and better provision for children to learn Sami languages. It adds that the Swedish government must uphold the Sami people’s right to practise reindeer husbandry and other cultural practices on their traditional lands.

The report concludes that the state, including the Swedish parliament, government and public authorities, and in some cases the Church of Sweden, must “bear responsibility” for policies and decisions that led to the violation of Sami rights.

It says: “Accepting responsibility also requires the state to work towards providing redress for the harm inflicted on the Sami people and individual Sami, while pursuing policies that do not repeat these historical injustices.”

articles.title: ‘He persuaded us’: Labour ministers moved by Andy Burnham’s emotional conference speech
articles.summary:
Prime minister’s pure political argument marks new era for party as he sets out his plans and priorities

The hottest ticket at Labour conference – after Andy Burnham’s speech – was an…

blocks.text: The hottest ticket at Labour conference – after Andy Burnham’s speech – was an afterparty in Liverpool’s Baltic Triangle, headlined with a set by the noughties girlband Sugababes. As Labour activists and ministers belted out the lyrics under pink spotlights, it was hard not to draw some parallels with the party’s recent history.
There have been painful lineup changes and a lot of internal division, but this week onstage in Liverpool the originals are back together and they only played the hits. The fans can’t get enough.

Burnham’s own show on the main stage had the conference hall in raptures not because of Brexit or social care but because of the display of raw emotion after the tightly choreographed repression of the last six years. He may as well have walked across the stage with his feet crunching over the debris of shattered Ming vases.

The speech combined plans that had been forming inside Burnham’s head for the last decade as well as seat-of-his-pants political instinct. On the morning of the conference, the prime minister took off early for a morning jog and then returned to make final amendments. Even moments before he went on stage, he was still rewriting, aides said. About a quarter of the speech was entirely ad-libbed.

When Burnham was rehearsing the speech, aides said, he knew he was going to cry when he got to the paragraph about his late father – he never managed to get through any of the practice runs without tears.

But the long pause as he composed himself was the most emotional he had been. Several ministers said they themselves had been moved to tears, including Ed Miliband, who had recently lost his mother, as well as Louise Haigh and Anneliese Midgley, who are Burnham’s closest friends in government and the architects of his ascendancy.

blocks.caption: All singing from the same hymn sheet? Burnham, with the Labour deputy leader, Lucy Powell, to his side, joins the traditional end-of-conference rendition of The Red Flag and Jerusalem.  Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian

blocks.text: After his speech, Burnham gathered all his ministers for a private pep talk. He said he knew they would not agree with everything, but – with the aura of a general sending his troops into battle – he told them to “get out there” and fight for it. He said he would not send them out with “a pea-shooter” – they needed proper weapons for the fight ahead and he promised he would provide them.
In the hallway outside the conference hall, minister after minister spoke with voices quivering with emotion. “This is all I have ever wanted,” one said.

The bar for speeches from political leaders has been low for the past decade or more. It is rare for clips to be anything more than a soundbite for social media and then a long shopping list of statistics and achievements. Burnham’s was the first time many MPs can recall a speech that was pure political argument.
And there was much in the speech that in normal times would have been a recipe for rebellion: Brexit, the triple lock, electoral reform and the lingering question marks over growth and defence.

“I found parts of the speech challenging, if I’m honest,” one cabinet minister admitted. “It contained things I had always thought we should never touch or an argument about public control which I would previously have said was too backward-looking. But in the room I agreed with every word because he persuaded us, he made an argument and made me question myself. It was a quite extraordinary thing.”
Even within the cabinet, there are those who grimace at the idea of electoral reform. “But you know, he believes in it, and I’m going to swallow it,” said one.

Burnham called his cabinet ministers in for a last-minute meeting just before the speech, where he laid out his private arguments and took their comments and feedback. “I feel almost embarrassed admitting this, but that has never happened before with any other leader,” one said.
after newsletter promotion

On the sidelines of the conference, when cabinet ministers are at their most candid, they sometimes talk as if they have been through a kind of collective trauma – and the Burnham ascendancy has given them the release they need to confess how hard they have found the last two years. There are close new friendships and alliances forged in the coup, which defy previous factional lines.

blocks.caption: A new togetherness? Close friendships and alliances have been forged in the party leadership coup. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian

blocks.text: “There’s the management-speak slogan: ‘Culture eats strategy for breakfast.’ Well, this is proof positive,” one cabinet minister said. “The past two years were utterly miserable, almost every single thing we achieved was poisoned by petty fighting. Every meeting was a choreographed exercise in pointlessness. Now we are discussing ideas and politics among colleagues who respect and like each other. I look back and I am so overwhelmed with relief that we did this.”

Another cabinet minister said: “I wasted so much of my own bandwidth fighting over the most puerile things, or defending my own staff who were being made miserable. Keir [Starmer] never dared to take it on.”

Even veterans of the Starmer years said they found themselves persuaded despite themselves. “Feels like there’s something quite psychologically profound about daring to take on the triple lock and finding that the planes don’t fall from the skies,” Starmer’s former strategy director Paul Ovenden posted.

Darren Jones, the ousted chief secretary who has made himself the face of the awkward squad, was also quick to lavish praise. “[The speech] told the story of his politics and the type of Britain he wants to build,” he said. “He told us we’d be in no doubt what his priorities are for the country, and he was right.”

Burnham will not welcome the comparison, but the closest recent one is how it felt at the Conservative party conference in the pre-disgrace Boris Johnson years: an electric electoral prospect who can genuinely reach across the political spectrum, hypnotising his doubters by the sheer force of his personality.

But this prime minister has no hint of the sleaze or incompetence that was always in the shadows for Johnson. If it comes, Burnham’s downfall will probably be his own voracious appetite for political risk – but that could also be the making of his premiership.

articles.title: African leaders herald $16B Dangote oil refinery in Kenya
articles.summary: An oil refinery on Kenya's coast is expected to be completed in 40 months, and will process an estimated 700,000 barrels of oil per day. Africa's richest man, Aliko Dangote, will lead the project.

image.caption: Ethiopia’s Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, Uganda’s President Yoweri Museveni and Kenya’s President William Ruto made a symbolic ceremony dig to celebrate the projectImage: Luis Tato/AFP

blocks.text: African leaders on Wednesday broke ground on a new $16 billion (€14 billion) oil refinery off Kenya's coast.
The project is expected to be completed in 40 months, and will process an estimated 700,000 barrels of oil per day. The refinery will be constructed at the coastal town of Lamu.

Kenya's President William Ruto, Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni, and Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed were among the leaders who attended an event to celebrate the project, the largest of its kind in East and Central Africa.
The refinery "will strengthen regional energy security, reduce reliance on imports and bolster our foreign exchange," Ruto said on social media.
"But this is more than a refinery. It is an integrated industrial complex featuring a 1,000MW power plant, plastic factory and the manufacturing of fertilizers and chemicals."
Africa's richest man, Nigerian industrialist Aliko Dangote, will oversee the project.
Dangote: Project will reduce refined fuel imports, foster self-sufficiency
Dangote said the refinery will make East Africa more "self-sufficient" by reducing imports of refined fuel.
"For too long, our continent has actually been rich in resources but poor in value creation and addition. We have exported crude oil and imported refined products," Dangote said in his speech.

"Such practice only leads to us exporting our jobs and opportunities that should remain on the continent and lead us into importing poverty into our nations. Africa cannot build lasting prospertiy by exporting what it has and importing what it needs," he continued.

blocks.caption: Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote (right) inspected earthmoving machinery with Kenyan President William Ruto (left)Image: Monicah Mwangi/REUTERS

blocks.text: Lamu project faces environmental concerns, legal challenge
The project, however, has faced resistance from environmental campaigners who fear it could harm Lamu Old Town, a UNESCO World Heritage Site which also hosts a fragile and unique marine ecosystem.
The Lamu marine environment is also home to animals such as dugongs, whales and various sea turtle species.

blocks.caption: The Lamu region is home to an incredible variety of aquatic life [FILE: October 4, 2011] Image: Thomas Mukoya/REUTERS

blocks.text: Lamu residents have brought a land rights legal case against the refinery, saying the site where it will be built is their ancestral heritage.
Kenya's High Court on Monday ruled that legal proceedings will continue, but the groundbreaking ceremony can take place.

articles.title: Ethiopia fighting escalates in Tigray killing 52 civilians, medic tells the BBC
articles.summary: The deadly fighting has also spread to neighbouring regions, stranding tourists in Lalibela.
articles.byline: Michael Teferi, Lion Tsigab, Lucy Fleming

blocks.text: At least 52 civilians have been killed during three days of heavy fighting around Alamata in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region, hospital sources have told the BBC.

It appears government troops have taken control of the town from regional fighters and intend to push north towards Mekelle, the region's main city. Social media clips show army tanks on Alamata's streets.
Clashes broke out last week after months of tension between the government and the party that controls Tigray, with both accusing each other of violating a 2022 deal that ended a two-year civil war.
Fighting has also affected neighbouring regions with 33 tourists stranded for the last week in Lalibela, a Unesco world heritage site.

"We have heard fighting, gunfire and artillery cannons firing throughout the week," a British tourist, who asked not to be named, told the BBC's Newsday programme about clashes near Lalibela in the Amhara region.
He said there was a large military presence in Lalibela, famous for being home to 13th Century churches hewn from rock and a holy site for millions of Orthodox Christians.

Most visitors to the tourist hub had been unable to leave since the airport closed to commercial flights last Wednesday, though he said 14 Israeli tourists had been evacuated by military helicopter on Monday.
The fighting around Lalibela has involved the army and an Amhara militia that has allied with Tigrayan fighters.
Earlier in September, they joined forces with other Ethiopian armed movements to form a seven-member alliance with the stated intention of removing the government in the capital, Addis Ababa.
There is also a fear that neighbouring Eritrea could be drawn into the conflict - as the government accuses Asmara of supporting the armed groups, something it denies.
The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas and it is difficult to find out what is happening because communications to the region have been cut.
The two sides disagree over who started the latest fighting.

The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray, says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in the region.
TPLF fighters are also fighting in the Afar region, in a strategic area which connects landlocked Ethiopia to Djibouti and its ports.
Over the last few days, medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said more than 700 wounded people had been admitted to hospitals it supports in Tigray.

The doctor at Alamata General Hospital, who requested anonymity, told the BBC the fighting in and around the town had taken place between Saturday and Monday, and involved heavy explosives and artillery, some of which landed in residential homes.
Those killed in the crossfire included children as young as three days old, mothers and cattle herders.
Twelve people had died in a single strike on the town's marketplace, the medic said.
Since the fighting erupted, banking services in Tigray have been suspended by the government. Access to the internet has also been cut - though it is not clear who ordered the closure.
A separate source in Alamata told the BBC there was a worsening humanitarian crisis in the area, as the town swelled with people fleeing fighting.
"All the residents of the surrounding areas entered the town of Alamata by walking on foot for as long as an hour, hoping the town would be safe.
"Unfortunately, everything is blocked - no banking service, no money transfer, no power, no internet, no phone. Hence people are in crisis, simply suffering, everyone is desperate and frustrated."
The British tourist in Lalibela said online banking was working in Lalibela but there was a shortage of physical cash.
He said the situation around the town had calmed down in the last two days and there were indications the airport, which was still being used by the military, might reopen on Thursday.
"The local people, they are still scared of what might happen. The military presence here in the town has remained and a larger military force has been seen leaving the town heading north," he said.
When the airport was first closed, 53 tourists had been in the town, he explained.
But some had since been evacuated, including the 14 Israelis airlifted out on Monday while another five had left the day before via an NGO convoy, despite advice not to travel by road.
Of the remaining tourists in Lalibela, the largest group were Americans, with Israelis, Britons, South Korean, South Africans, an Ethiopian-New Zealander and a Mexican also stranded, he said.
Meanwhile, for those cut off in Tigray because of the telecoms shutdown, the Tigray Broadcasting Service (TBS), based in Addis Ababa, has started an initiative to help reconnect families.
The broadcaster has said it will collect video messages via its Telegram channel from people outside the region and air them via satellite TV.
While limited to greetings and updates, this will provide a rare lifeline for families separated by the blackout.
The clampdown on Tigray's banking services is also affecting Tigrayans who are not physically in the region.
Customers have told the BBC that bank accounts opened in Tigray have been frozen or restricted.

"I boarded public transport from Addis Ababa to Adama and tried to pay using a mobile transfer, but it didn't work," said a former Mekelle resident who moved to the capital two months ago because of growing tensions in Tigray.
"It has created havoc for many people like me who escaped the situation in Tigray," he told the BBC's Tigrinya service.
"Many Tigrayans are now in trouble."
Additional reporting by Yemane Nagish
