articles.title: Gracioso takes 2nd lie detector test at NBI
articles.summary: Dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. took a lie detector test before the National Bureau of Investigation on Wednesday, September 30.

blocks.text: Published September 30, 2026 8:54pm
Dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. took a lie detector test before the National Bureau of Investigation on Wednesday, September 30.
According to NBI Director Melvin Matibag, Gracioso voluntarily took the test, which was his second with the NBI.
Matibag said the process took three hours, from 3:30 p.m. to 6:30 p.m.
The NBI is investigating claims Gracioso made in an affidavit that he delivered bags of cash to Vice President Sara Duterte while he was a security aide to former Speaker Lord Allan Velasco.
Officials mentioned in Gracioso's affidavit have denied his allegations.
Matibag has said Gracioso approached the bureau with the help of Father Flavie Villanueva, a priest known for assisting families of victims of the Duterte administration’s drug war.
He said the NBI had checked Gracioso’s background and was examining his claims through interviews and other investigative means.
Matibag also cited the first polygraph test administered to Gracioso.

“Ang masasabi ko nga, based on the test that we ran, which is the polygraph test, 99% yung truthfulness ng kanyang mga statements.” (Based on the polygraph test we ran, I would say there was 99% truthfulness in his statements.)
The Supreme Court in People v. Adoviso held that lie detector test results are not admissible as evidence in court to prove the guilt or innocence of an accused in criminal cases.
This is due to a lack of scientific acceptance.

“However, polygraph tests when offered in evidence for the purpose of establishing the guilt or innocence of one accused of a crime, whether the accused or the prosecution seeks its introduction, for the reason that polygraph has not as yet attained scientific acceptance as a reliable and accurate means of ascertaining truth or deception,” the SC said.
For the SC, lie detector test results are not conclusive.

“While the Court held that the results of a polygraph test cannot be offered in evidence to prove the guilt or innocence of an accused in a crime, it does not mean that it has no weight at all,” it said.
“The results of the polygraph test may be used in conjunction with other corroborative evidence to prove an allegation made by a party,” it added. —NB, GMA News

articles.title: Burundi agrees to receive ‘third-country’ migrant deportees from US
articles.summary:
Burundi joins several other African nations in accepting people deported under Trump’s hardline policy

Burundi has agreed to join a…

blocks.text: Burundi has agreed to join a clutch of ⁠other African nations in receiving migrants from other countries deported from the US under ⁠Donald Trump’s hardline ⁠immigration ​policy.

However, the authorities in Bujumbura, the country’s economic capital, said Burundi will only accept those not accused of crime or terrorism links, said ⁠Nancy Ninette Mutoni, a spokesperson for the country’s president, Évariste Ndayishimiye. Tuesday’s announcement gave no details of numbers, timing or financial ⁠details.

Washington has sent so-called “third-country deportees” to some half ​a dozen African nations ‌as well as many other countries, often where they have no ties, have never been and find themselves detained indefinitely, under opaque deals ‌that Senate Democrats say have cost tens of millions of ‌dollars.

In many cases, deportees had secured legal protections from immigration courts in the US against repatriation. But rights groups say the third-country deals allow the US to circumvent those protections.

Mutoni said preparations were underway to arrange accommodation, ‌living conditions and integration into local communities in Burundi. “Receiving them requires serious planning – where they will stay, what they ​will eat and how they will live alongside the local population,” she said.
“If they choose to join Burundian citizens and make a valuable contribution to national development, the law ⁠will be respected,” she said, regarding potential citizenship.
Burundi aimed ​to both ​strengthen diplomatic relations and provide ​hospitality to people in need, the spokesperson ​added.
The US ‌state department ​did not ​immediately respond to requests for comment while a spokesperson for the Burundi foreign ministry said details of the agreement were not yet available.

articles.title: Bosnia elections: Polls overshadowed by exhaustion, exodus and geopolitics as ethnic politics eclipse real problems
articles.summary: Bosnia goes to the polls on October 4 to elect several parliaments and presidents. While voters worry about the economy and emigration, the campaign is focused on ethnicity, exposing the country's…

image.caption: General elections are being held in Bosnia and Herzegovina on October 4Image: Denis Zuberi/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: Picture a country that has lost nearly one in six of its citizens — roughly 600,000 people —through emigration in just ten years.
A country that has conducted only a single census since being ravaged by war in the 1990s, counting just over 3.5 million people in 2013.

A country where young people aged 20 to 29 are leaving faster than any other age group and where demographers warn of a looming population collapse because the birth rate has trailed the mortality rate every year since 2009.
This is Bosnia and Herzegovina.

But when voters here go to the polls on October 4 to elect people to the most powerful positions at both state and entity levels, the focus of the election campaign will not be on how to stop the country hemorrhaging citizens. It will — once again and for the umpteenth time — be about who is Serb, who is Bosniak, who is Croat and who supposedly threatens whom.
That fact alone says more about the state of Bosnian politics than any opinion poll could.
A complicated electoral system

After the brutal 1992-95 Bosnian War, Bosnia and Herzegovina was left divided by the Dayton Peace Agreement — a compromise that stopped the killing but built ethnicity into the state's architecture as a permanent rather than a temporary fix.
Three decades on, that architecture hasn't changed, and progress has stalled completely.
The complicated constitution drafted at Dayton produced an equally complicated electoral system.

Bosnia is divided into two entities, the Serb-majority Republika Srpska and the Bosniak-Croat Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the Brcko District. It has a total of 14 governments and parliaments at state, entity and cantonal level — a lot for such a small country.

On October 4, voters will elect a new presidency at state level. The presidency in Bosnia comprises three people. Each of the three ethnic groups elects its own representative: a Serb chosen in Republika Srpska, and a Bosniak and a Croat chosen in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

blocks.caption: Research shows that ethnic identity remains the single strongest predictor of how people in Bosnia voteImage: Dragan Maksimović/DW

blocks.text: On top of that, voters will be electing a new president in Republika Srpska and lawmakers for both the state-level and entity parliaments, while the Federation's president and the remaining parliamentary chambers are filled after the vote through ethnic quotas.
Voting along ethnic lines
Bosnia today operates as a patchwork of parallel, ethnically defined power structures whose chief skill is blocking one another. And that isn't a design flaw, it's the design.

"Many citizens will keep voting for parties that represent their own people, because political elites constantly manufacture a sense of threat and fear, turning elections into a referendum on national survival," political scientist Mladen Bubonjic told DW.

This is far removed from the issues affecting voters in their day-to-day lives: high prices, low wages and pensions, unaffordable housing, precarious jobs, corruption, poor public services and the steady drain of people leaving the country.
Same script, new faces
Poll after poll shows that voters don't believe campaign promises, and their answers in such polls tend to boil down to the same thing: "Nothing has changed in 30 years."

blocks.caption: Voters will elect the members of the presidency and parliaments in the two entities that make up the country and at cantonal level. Pictured here: the buildings of the Council of Ministers and Bosnian parliament in Sarajevo Image: Dragan Maksimović/DW

blocks.text: That sentence could have been spoken a decade ago, or even two decades ago. And that's precisely the problem: Bosnian politics isn't stuck by accident, it's stuck by design, because the system rewards whoever keeps the divisions alive and punishes anyone who tries to make meaningful change.

Elections in Bosnia have never simply been about getting better roads or cheaper electricity. They function as an act of tribal defense, and every side knows it and cultivates it. Research consistently shows that ethnic identity remains the single strongest predictor of how people vote, far outweighing economic self-interest.

This campaign, too, has been dominated by identity politics and institutional paralysis rather than any real debate over jobs or prices. This means voters are choosing fear, because no one is seriously offering them a real alternative.

"Unfortunately, out of a decades-old habit, ethnic tensions keep rallying citizens around ideological and identity issues. Corruption, poverty and demographic collapse have all been absorbed into political identities," political analyst Tanja Topic told DW.
What voters actually want fixed

But step off the political stage and onto the street and people's priorities sound the same as they do in any other country: They want jobs, a paycheck that covers the bills, an affordable home, healthcare that actually works and a government that doesn't steal.

blocks.caption: Voters would like to see politicians tackling a range of subjects such as high prices, low wages and pensions, housing, public services and emigrationImage: Dragan Maksimovic/DW

blocks.text: People blame corruption as the reason reforms stall before they are completed, and young people choose to leave the country rather than cast a ballot.
The real fight is over identity and wartime history, not economic hardship. Migration gets mentioned mostly as an alarming statistic, rarely as an issue anyone is racing to solve.

"The Bosnian triangle, dominated by three ethnic principles, is disastrous for all of Bosnia's citizens. But if you don't vote along those lines, you get branded a traitor to your own people. Which is disastrous for the country's progress," Vehid Sehic, a political analyst from Tuzla, told DW.
EU accession recedes further into the distance
Bosnia has been an EU candidate since 2022. In 2024, it got the green light to open accession talks. In practice, however, progress along that path has all but ground to a halt.

An independent analysis shows that, according to the EU's own progress reports, Bosnia's readiness score dropped from 4.14 to 2.91 out of ten in a single year — the steepest fall of any candidate country.
Bosnia still hasn't appointed a chief negotiator for EU accession talks, and of the 113 reforms required for EU accession, not one has been implemented.

blocks.caption: Bosnia has been an EU candidate since 2022, but implementation of the necessary reforms required for accession has stagnated. Pictured here: EU High Representative Kaja Kallas (left) and Chairwoman of the Council of Ministers of Bosnia, Borjana KristoImage: Council of Ministers of BiH

blocks.text: For ordinary citizens, EU membership is no longer a burning question. It has curdled into a tired, accepted truth that when politicians speak of the "European path," it amounts to little more than ink on paper.
Geopolitical backdrop

Bosnia's elections, alongside Serbia's on October 25, are taking place at a time when the Western Balkans has once again become a stage for intense rivalry between Russia, the European Union and the United States.
Against this backdrop, political forces across Bosnia are already looking for allies abroad.

Bosnia is heading into this election as a country that has spent three decades spinning in place, at the exact moment its internal paralysis has turned it into a playing field for other people's geopolitical bets.
Meanwhile, the 600,000 people who have already left in search of a normal life have effectively answered the question of whether they think anything is about to change.

articles.title: Botswana condemned for slaughtering elephants for independence celebrations
articles.summary: The government authorises the hunting of 23 elephants and dozens of other wild animals for independence day feasts.

blocks.text: Animal rights activists have criticised Botswana's decision to authorise the killing of 23 elephants to provide meat for independence celebrations.
The southern African country, home to the world's largest elephant population, is holding nationwide festivities on Wednesday to mark the 60th anniversary of independence from Britain.
A licence issued by the Ministry of Environment and Tourism, seen by local media, authorises the hunting of 23celephants and other wild animals for "complimentary purposes".
The Botswana-based Elephant Protection Society warns the decision could undermine conservation, with its chairman Oaitse Nawa telling the BBC elephants needed greater protection.
He warned that slaughtering elephants for celebratory feasting could encourage poaching by creating the impression that killing elephants is acceptable when sanctioned by government.
"Elephants have lost their social structures because they are always being pushed from one place to another by gunshots," Nawa said.

Several social media users in the country have also expressed concerns about eating the game meat amid an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease, which has prompted authorities to impose measures to contain its spread.
Tshenatshe Monwela, an elder in Maun, a tourism town in north-western Botswana told local media that his community should have received buffalo instead.

He argued that elephants had particular cultural and ecological significance and that Botswana's historic role in protecting the country's wildlife and livestock should have been recognised in the government's allocation of meat for the anniversary celebrations.

Botswana's government has organised a series of events to mark the country's diamond jubilee, including a carnival in the capital, Gaborone, as well as cultural performances, concerts and sporting events.
The game meat is expected to be served as part of the traditional feasting associated with the Independence Day celebrations.
The 23 elephants were allocated in eight districts across the country.
It was not immediately clear how many of the animals had been killed by Wednesday morning. The BBC has asked the government for comment.
But local media published images from different parts of Botswana showing residents gathering around elephant carcasses, some with knives in hand and sharing the meat.

In Chobe, a wildlife-rich district in northern Botswana near the borders with Namibia, Zambia and Zimbabwe, a local MP raised concerns after residents reportedly collected portions directly from a carcass at a school.

He said the system risked creating congestion and disadvantaging elderly people, pregnant women and people with disabilities, and suggested the meat should instead be processed into 5kg or 10kg packages to improve hygiene and ensure fairer distribution.

"For the sake of dignity, fairness and public hygiene, we respectfully call on the hunter and the relevant leadership to ensure that future distributions are properly organised," MP Simasiku Mapulanga posted on Facebook, attaching photos of people scrambling for meat around an elephant carcass.
Elephant meat is common in some wildlife-rich communities, particularly when meat from legal hunts is distributed locally, but it is not an everyday staple.
Botswana also tightly regulates game meat, and its legal possession generally depends on proving it came from a lawful hunt.
The decision has reignited a long-running and often heated debate in Botswana over how the country manages its huge elephant population.
Botswana has more than 130,000 elephants and communities living alongside them have long complained about animals destroying crops, damaging property and sometimes killing people.
The government has defended regulated hunting as one way of managing the elephant population and human-wildlife conflict while generating income for communities.
The country banned trophy hunting in 2014 under former President Ian Khama but lifted the restrictions five years later under his successor, Mokgweetsi Masisi.
Hunting has continued under President Duma Boko, who defeated Masisi in elections in 2024.
The government says proceeds from hunting supports conservation and local development.
Minister of Environment and Tourism Wynter Mmolotsi told parliament last year that special elephant quotas raised 15.6m pula ($1.1m; £820,000) in 2025 for projects in areas where elephants are found.
But conservation organisations have questioned whether the level of hunting is sustainable.

Supporters of Botswana's hunting policy, however, argue that international criticism often overlooks the costs borne by rural communities living alongside one of the world's biggest concentrations of elephants.
They say elephants destroy crops and infrastructure and pose a danger to people, particularly as their range increasingly overlaps with farms and settlements.

articles.title: In the Public Square: Taking the fight to the dynasties
articles.summary: How did Philippine politics get this way? And what can be done to change it?

blocks.text: How did Philippine politics get this way? And what can be done to change it?

In the ongoing drama of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, the Senate sits as the impeachment court—and also as a representative of the general public. But the Senate also represents the country in a different and darker way: It is the practice of dynasty politics taken to the extreme.

Eight seats in the 24-person Senate are occupied by four pairs of siblings. At least four are held by senators who have family members in national elective or appointive positions. At least two belong to political families.
It is time to take the fight to the dynasties.

In this new episode of In the Public Square, Rappler columnist John Nery is joined by former Supreme Court senior associate justice Antonio Carpio, and lawyer Alex Lacson, the chair and vice chair, respectively, of the People’s Initiative Coalition Against Dynasties.

articles.title: Top Trump figures push to direct human rights funding to rightwing causes
articles.summary:
Support for white Afrikaners, anti-communism and others reveals how US redefining what qualifies as human rights

With hours left before the funding expires, the Trump administration is…
articles.byline: Andrew Roth and Joseph Gedeon in Washington

blocks.text: With hours left before the funding expires, the Trump administration is pushing to direct more than $175m of the state department’s flagship human rights fund to a slate of awards that includes a massive $40m grant for an anti-communism fund, support for a group advancing white Afrikaner rights in South Africa, a campaign against Brazil’s supreme court, and programs that would reward ideological allies in Europe who protect “western civilisational norms”.

Critics have focused on 43 awards of a combined $176.9m that will bolster rightwing and conservative causes around the world while likely angering US allies over interference in internal politics. The Guardian has seen a sample of the controversial grants, which makes up most of the $205m in funding that Congress has appropriated for the entire human rights and democracy fund (HRDF).

Sources with knowledge of the grant process have told the Guardian that the awards were personally lobbied for by members of the Trump administration, and reflect interests that include JD Vance’s warnings of the collapse of traditional western values in Europe, and Stephen Miller’s push against immigration and to support white minorities in countries like South Africa.

“The story for me is the high-level – including White House-directed – attention on these programs,” said a person familiar with the discussions over the democracy awards. “These awards have been briefed at the highest levels of the department and have buy-in from the White House.”

The proposed awards represent a significant shift in US support for dissidents, human-rights defenders and civil-society groups under authoritarian governments. The new slate includes projects in wealthy nations, and focused on opposition to regulation, Brexit, migration, anti-communism, Christian protection and opposition to “gender ideology”, offering a window into how the Trump administration is redefining what qualifies as human rights and merits tens of millions of dollars in US foreign assistance.

“Congress appropriated money for the democracy fund on a bipartisan basis to support defenders of human rights, to assist victims of human rights violations and to instead promote the growth of democracy abroad,” said senator Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the US Senate committee on foreign relations.

“The Trump administration’s proposals would use taxpayer funds to promote far-right organizations and programs in established democracies. This is a waste of resources and undermines United States values and relations with democratic partners, including allies in Europe.”

The largest award of $40m was directed to a consortium led by the Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation (VOC), an anti-communist non-profit that has received far smaller grants in the past. A state department vetting document seen by the Guardian records $96,997 in previous contracts in the last five years between the foundation and the department, all in the 2022 fiscal year, and notes that it had been vetted in 2019 in connection with tickets to the foundation’s gala. The vetting document also identifies Andrew Bremberg, a former Trump White House domestic policy adviser and US ambassador to the UN European office, as a “senior leader” of the foundation.

In July, ProPublica reported that Samuel Samson, a 27-year-old deputy assistant secretary overseeing the new grants, was linked to senior members of VOC through his studies at the Christian conservative Hillsdale College graduate program. (A state department official then told the outlet that the relationship had nothing to do with the grant).

Samson has described the US and Europe as partners in a shared civilizational struggle. Samson toured Austria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia last December – all countries that were floated to receive a $2m grant to counter migration weaponized by Russia and Belarus, and criticized NGOs that previous administrations had worked with for promoting what he called radical concepts, including gender theory and DEI.

The state department did not comment on individual grants but told the Guardian the programs were still in “active deliberation”, that awardees would meet guidelines for federal grants, and that all programming would undergo a “standard and rigorous vetting process by grant professionals.”

“Our programming in Europe aims to support our European allies in defending those rights and principles, along with their civilizational self-confidence and sovereignty from those who seek to undermine them,” a state department official said. “The national security strategy highlights our priorities in Europe which includes advancing political liberty, promoting free speech, and collaborating with European partners to jointly support European revitalization and civilizational self-confidence.”

Under the legislation authorizing the fund, the money must be assigned by 30 September, the end of the fiscal year, when unobligated funds typically lapse. Shaheen, the ranking member of the Senate foreign relations committee, has put a partial “hold” on giving the grants to some of the controversial awardees – setting up a showdown with the State Department with just hours left for the money to be obligated.
ProPublica first reported that Trump officials had drawn up at least a dozen no-bid grants aimed at rightwing and anti-immigration causes in Europe and advocates for white South Africans.
The document now shows how much of the fund the plan takes up, and which awards have since been dropped.

A $1m award titled “Countering Lawfare and Censorship in Brazil” would fund civil society groups opposing what it calls judicial overreach and censorship by Brazil’s supreme court. The Trump administration sanctioned Justice Alexandre de Moraes last year after lobbying by Eduardo Bolsonaro, son of the former president.

A program titled “Promoting Western Civilization Allies” would be limited to implementers who do not subscribe to “ideologically weaponized accounts of human rights, such as gender ideology”, according to the document, and will receive $2m. It names possible recipients in Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and the Balkans with “anti-communist” and “natural rights” approaches.

One award was allocated to document “democratic backsliding” in Europe tied to “mass and illegal migration” and legislation by “supra-national entities”, while a $1m journalism consortium would push back against designations of “trusted” media outlets. The list also includes $2m for early-warning networks protecting Christians in Nigeria.

And a $3m no-bid award would go to the Jobs Foundation, a UK group run by Matthew Elliott, who led the Vote Leave campaign. The grant, titled “Countering Overregulation to Advance American Investment”, would promote a “common good capitalism index” and pro-business policy, including how the foundation promoted Brexit as a chance to cut the UK’s climate regulations.

The document also shows that a proposed $5m no-bid grant to the Free Speech Union, the British group founded by Toby Young, has been marked “withdrawn”. When the award was first reported in July, Young said the group had never applied for or received US government money (though Trump officials had reportedly met with the group during a European tour late last year).

The grant would have paid the group to campaign against online safety and hate speech laws, including Britain’s Online Safety Act, a law passed under the Conservatives in 2023. Meant to protect children from harmful content and is enforced by Ofcom, its age-verification rules – which took effect last year – have drawn constant criticism from the Trump administration, which cast them as censorship.

The Free Speech Union is the second British group to drop off the list. A $7m no-bid award to 878, a thinktank whose stated missions include restoring Judeo-Christian culture and “ending mass migration and deporting illegal immigrants”, was abandoned in July after pushback from Congress. It was founded by Jacob Rees-Mogg, who served as Brexit opportunities minister and business secretary before losing his seat at the 2024 election, and now presents on GB News.

The British awards would have sent $15m in US taxpayer money to groups run by two sitting Conservative peers and a former cabinet minister, on issues from online safety law to migration that are live in British politics.

articles.title: Russia launches largest attack on Ukraine energy infrastructure since spring
articles.summary: At least six people were killed and 33 others injured across the country in the overnight attacks, local authorities reported.

blocks.text: Russia has launched the largest attack on Ukraine's energy infrastructure since the spring, primarily targeting Kyiv and the surrounding region, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskyi has said.
At least six people were killed and 33 others injured across the country in the overnight attacks, including a child in the Kyiv region, local authorities reported.
The strikes also impacted people's power supplies, with Ukraine's biggest private energy firm, DTEK, saying power to 8,000 homes had been restored following "a difficult night" for the capital.
The Russian defence ministry said one of its targets was the Trypilska power station, the largest supplier of electricity to Kyiv. This has not been confirmed by Ukrainian officials.
In a statement on Telegram, Koretskyi said: "Since the summer, there has effectively not been a single day without enemy attacks on our energy infrastructure.
"However, a mass and combined attack of this scale has occurred for the first time since the end of the last heating season."
Ukraine has been expecting another protracted Russian assault on the country's energy grid. It has happened every winter so far since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
In total 11 regions of the country were attacked overnight, with residential buildings, social infrastructure, civilian enterprises and railways also targeted, Koretskyi said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said there were strikes on critical infrastructure in the Zhytomyr, Mykolaiv, Kirovohrad and Rivne regions.
On Wednesday, some households in the Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Sumy, Kyiv and Kharkiv regions remained without power, Ukraine's energy ministry said.
State-owned grid operator Ukrenegro advised residents not to use powerful electrical appliances between the hours of 10:00 and 16:00 local time as electricity supplies were lower than usual.

In Kyiv, people woke to find the city blanketed by thick, acrid smoke after a night punctuated by the sound of explosions. An air raid alert was still on and the distant sound of air defence gunfire echoed through the murky atmosphere.
Residents in several districts were advised to close their windows until the smoke cleared.
Among those killed in the overnight strikes was a child whose body was found under the rubble of a house, Kyiv regional governor Timur Tkachenko said.

Kyiv Mayor Vitaly Klischko said three people were killed in total in the capital, including a Ukrainian utility company worker who was killed at a warehouse building. It is not clear if the three he mentioned included the child.
Two people were also killed in the north-eastern Sumy region, governor Oleh Hryhorov said, while another person was killed in the Mykolaiv region, acting regional governor Heorhiy Reshetilov said.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

articles.title: Israeli minister claims ‘terrorist’ wanted to crash plane after Israel-bound flight’s emergency landing – latest
articles.summary: Israeli media say incident, which raised fears of possible hijacking, stemmed from feud between plane’s two pilots

blocks.text: Key events

items: 23m agoIsraeli minister claims 'terrorist' attempted to crash plane bound for Tel Aviv

blocks.text: Israeli minister claims 'terrorist' attempted to crash plane bound for Tel Aviv

An Israeli minister has decried what he described as a “terrorist” incident to kill Israelis after a flight was forced to land in Saudi Arabia when a physical altercation between the pilot and co-pilot prompted initial fears of a hijacking.

A Boeing 737 Max 8 with up to 180 passengers on board made an emergency landing at Saudi Arabia’s Tabuk airport this morning after transmitting three emergency signals, one of which indicated what is known as a possible unlawful interference. Israeli media have reported dramatic testimonies and video from people on board, with some describing passengers storming the cockpit to subdue the attacker and one of the pilots being seriously injured.

blocks.caption: Passengers aboard the Boeing 737 Max 8 travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv told Israeli media that one of the pilots tried to crash the plane before being overpowered. Photograph: Amit Segal

blocks.text: The Israeli national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, said the incident highlighted the need for Israel to escalate its military campaigns across the region.

“Thank God and the heroic passengers, but Israel’s security doctrine must be taken to the next level,” he wrote on X, adding that the country “must continue until achieving total victory” in Iran, Lebanon, Gaza and the occupied West Bank.

“The naive notion that our enemies value life and deserve our pity was given yet another stark reminder this morning in the form of a terrorist who planned to blow up a plane and murder the 180 Israelis on board.”

Similarly, the Israeli finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, said that “anyone who tried to bring down a plane and murder 180 Israelis should pay as though they had murdered them – as should any country or terrorist organisation that sent them”.

According to the Israeli Hareetz newspaper, citing an unnamed official, authorities were treating it as a “terror” incident and “believe that one of the pilots may have purposefully attempted to crash the plane”. The newspaper added that other scenarios were also being considered.

Commenting this morning, the Israeli prime minister’s office said the situation was “under control” while measures are being taken to bring the passengers to Israel. Local media reported the military had scrambled fighter jets after fears of a possible hijacking, which the prime minister’s office had ruled out shortly after the incident came to light.
In a statement, Tabuk airport said the flight that was bound for Tel Aviv landed at 9.45am local time and that its captain and co-pilot “were found to have injuries and were transported to hospital”.
FlyDubai said flight FZ 1073 “experienced an incident while en route” and that all passengers “are safe and accounted for”.

articles.title: Last UK and US troops leave Iraq as anti-Islamic State mission ends
articles.summary: The withdrawal of coalition forces, under a deal agreed two years ago, was a key demand of the Iraqi government.

blocks.text: The last British and American troops have left Iraq after a military presence of more than a decade in the country.
The exit of the remaining UK military personnel - around 100 - from Irbil, in the northern Kurdistan region, was co-ordinated over recent weeks with US forces, who also departed on Wednesday.
It follows an agreement between the US and the Iraqi government, signed two years ago, to withdraw foreign troops by the end of this month.

British and US forces have been present in Iraq since 2014, as part of the international coalition to help defeat the extremist Islamic State (IS) group. Their departure brings the mission, known as Operation Inherent Resolve, to an end.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said the end of the coalition's mission marked "Iraq's transition to a phase in which it assumes full responsibility for its security and stability".
Iraq is set to hold four "Sovereignty Days" as a national holiday to mark the withdrawal.

"Following more than a decade of operations, training and capacity building, Iraqi Security Forces (ISF) and the Kurdish Peshmerga have secured the enduring territorial defeat of Daesh in Iraq and are now well placed to take primary responsibility for the country's security," the UK Ministry of Defence (MoD) said in a statement, referring to IS by an Arabic acronym.
"With these objectives achieved, Iraq and its international partners can begin a new chapter focused on enduring security co-operation under Iraqi leadership."
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said the coalition's departure from Irbil marked "the successful conclusion of the military mission that defeated [IS] in Iraq".

He added: "The primary responsibility for addressing Iraq's remaining security challenges, including [IS] remnants and Iran-aligned militias that undermine Iraqi sovereignty and regional stability, now rests with the government of Iraq."
The Iraqi government declared the military defeat of IS in 2017, but coalition forces remained to help prevent the group's resurgence.
A recent UN report estimated that sustained counter-terrorism pressure by Iraqi security forces had left IS with several hundred fighters who were "able to carry out unsophisticated operations only".
The Iraqi government also faces the challenge of Iranian-backed militias in the country.
Zaidi, who took office in May, has vowed to disarm them and bring all weapons under state control following the coalition's exit.
But several powerful factions have resisted his plans and could now see their influence grow without the US presence.
Since the start of the US and Israel's war with Iran earlier this year, militias have been targeting the remaining US and UK forces stationed at Irbil air base.
Hundreds of Nato troops stationed in Baghdad left the country in March as tensions rose.
A BBC team visited the coalition base in Irbil in April this year, during a fragile ceasefire between the US and Iran.
They were forced to circle the base in an RAF transport aircraft while drones were being launched nearby.
At the height of the US bombing campaign against Iran, the coalition base was being targeted by up to 28 drones and missiles a day.

RAF Regiment Gunners, who were among the last British military personnel stationed there, had shot down more than 100 drones in the first six weeks of the war. Many of the attack drones were being launched by Iranian-backed militias in Iraq.
On Wednesday, signalling the end of the mission, the MoD paid tribute to UK personnel who had contributed to the counter-IS mission.

It said they had provided "valuable support, training and assistance" to more than 111,000 members of the Iraqi Security Forces, including more than 21,000 Peshmerga forces in the semi-autonomous Kurdistan Region.

It also said the RAF had conducted thousands of sorties, striking more than 2,300 IS targets. The RAF is expected to continue flying missions over neighbouring Syria, to prevent the remnants of IS from gaining a foothold.
The Pentagon said the US would continue to provide "targeted training and intelligence support" to its Iraqi partners.
US Central Command said the coalition's joint taskforce remained operational and was now based in Jordan.
US forces will also continue their mission against IS in Syria, where the UN estimates that the group has up to 3,000 fighters.
This is the third time US and UK forces have withdrawn from Iraq.
Tens of thousands of US and British troops were deployed to the country in 1991 following Saddam Hussein's invasion of Kuwait.

They returned to Iraq in 2003, when US President George W Bush ordered Operation Iraqi Freedom to remove the dictator from power and eliminate weapons of mass destruction that turned out not to exist.
The fierce sectarian insurgency that engulfed Iraq following the invasion cost tens of thousands of lives, including those of nearly 4,500 US military personnel and 179 British military personnel.
US and UK forces left Iraq in 2011, only to return three years later, when IS threatened to take control of the country.

articles.title: Chasing her ‘best version,’ Alex Eala reaches Asian Games semis for sure medal
articles.summary: Alex Eala knows the risk of losing, but that mindset keeps her at the top of her game as she disposes of Chinese Taipei's Joanna Garland to secure at least a bronze in the 2026 Asian Games

blocks.text: CROWD DARLING. Tennis player Alex Eala in action for the Philippines in the 2026 Asian Games.
PSC-POC Media Pool
Alex Eala knows the risk of losing, but that mindset keeps her at the top of her game as she disposes of Chinese Taipei's Joanna Garland to secure at least a bronze in the 2026 Asian Games

items: Alex Eala, the favorite for the gold medal in the Asian Games, acknowledges the possibility of losing despite her strong performance.
Eala advanced to the semifinals after defeating Joanna Garland, showcasing her resilience and ability to overcome challenges during the match.
With top competitors absent from the tournament, Eala is positioned as a leading contender for the gold medal as she prepares to face Wang Xiyu in the next round.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – As much as Alex Eala is the favorite to win the gold medal in the Asian Games, she remains mindful of the possibility of losing.

Upsets in tennis are not uncommon, with the world No. 18 Filipina fresh from a surprise exit in the Singapore Open, where she fell to Russia’s Tatiana Prozorova in a defeat that marked the first time she lost to a player outside the world top 100 since she broke into the top 50.

But that understanding has kept Eala at the top of her game as she assured herself of a medal in the 2026 Asian Games after advancing to the semifinals of the women’s singles event following a 7-5, 6-0 win over Chinese Taipei’s Joanna Garland at the Higashiyama Park Tennis Center on Wednesday, September 30.

“And at the end of the day, being a professional tennis player and a competitive tennis player, losing comes. You have to understand that losing is part of the job and losing is always a possibility,” Eala said after the match.

“That’s what makes tennis so difficult, that’s what makes tennis so exciting, is that you never know what’s going to happen and you can’t let your guard down. I think that also contributes to my pursuit for excellence and my pursuit for the best version of myself.”

Ranked 143rd in the world, Garland held her own against the top-seeded Filipina in the first half of the match that took 1 hour and 49 minutes to finish, even grabbing a 5-4 lead to move on the brink of stealing the opening set.
But Eala found another gear, winning the next three games to clinch the first set and dominate the rest of the way.

Eala won nine consecutive games in total as she served her second bagel of the Asian Games after opening the tournament with a 6-1, 6-0 shellacking of Thailand’s Patcharin Cheapchandej on Monday, September 28.
“I ended the match playing better than I started, which is always a good thing,” Eala, who secured at least a bronze, told Cignal. “Really happy with the win.”
Eala took home a bronze in the 2023 edition, where she lost in the semifinals to eventual champion Zheng Qinwen of China.

This time, Zheng is not around, as well as other top Asian players in world No. 1 Elena Rybakina of Kazakhstan and No. 17 Naomi Osaka of Japan as they opted to see action in the China Open, leaving Eala as the leading gold-medal contender.
Eala shoots for a spot in the final as she battles world No. 49 Wang Xiyu of China next. – Rappler.com

articles.title: AI tool that copied actor’s ‘lustrous’ voice violated his rights, says Tokyo court
articles.summary:
Kenjiro Tsuda wins case against TikTok account in landmark verdict to protect publicity rights

A court in Japan has ruled that the human…

blocks.text: A court in Japan has ruled that the human voice has legal protection after a landmark case involving a well-known actor and a TikTok account that he claimed had cloned his “lustrous” baritone voice in its AI-generated videos.

Tokyo district court said on Wednesday that voices should enjoy the same protection as publicity rights, at the end of a closely watched legal action brought against TikTok by Kenjiro Tsuda – best known for voicing the character Kento Nanami in the anime Jujutsu Kaisen.

But the court dismissed Tsuda’s request that the operator of TikTok remove the videos, noting that the user had deleted them soon after the suit was filed last November. “The unauthorised use of a performer’s voice … can be considered an infringement on publicity rights,” said the presiding judge, Aya Takahashi.

The lawsuit is believed to be the first in Japan seeking to defend an individual’s vocal identity against AI-generated copies. Japan’s voice actors, many of whom achieve star status through their “appearances” in anime, are increasingly worried that AI mimicry is threatening their livelihoods and the industry as a whole.
An actor’s voice “is the result of years of rigorous training and apprenticeship”, Yuko Sasaki, executive director of the Japan Actors Union said ahead of the ruling.

Tsuda, 55, claimed that the 188 TikTok videos uploaded on an anonymous account between July 2024 and September last year had been narrated by a “deep” and “lustrous” voice that could only be his. In response, the platform argued that the videos contained a “generic male voice” and that any perceived similarities to Tsuda’s voice were highly subjective.

The verdict is the first in which a Japanese court has declared that the human voice is protected under publicity rights, a reference to the ability to control and profit from aspects of an individual’s identity, in Tsuda’s case his distinctive voice.

The protection applies “if the purpose of using the voice is exclusively to take advantage of its commercial appeal”, Takahashi said, describing a voice to be “as symbolic of one’s personality as portraits are”.
The TikTok account, whose picture resembled Tsuda’s Jujutsu Kaisen character, combined images and AI-generated speech about urban legends, the occult and conspiracy theories.

At one point, the account had more than 200,000 subscribers and, according to the legal complaint, the clips would have earned its owner between ¥500,000 (£2,395) and ¥75,000 in monthly revenue, the Kyodo news agency said.
after newsletter promotion
Describing the content as “sordid”, Tsuda’s legal team claimed the account had only attracted attention because it had cloned the “attractive voice of a popular actor”.

TikTok said in a statement it would “respect the court’s judgment while considering what steps to take after scrutinising [the ruling’s] details”. It added: “We will continue to sincerely work on the balance between technology development and rights protection.”
In 2024, actors in Japan launched a campaign called “No More” to oppose the unauthorised use of their faces and voices in AI-generated content.
With reporting by Agence France-Presse

The units contained amenities including air conditioners, big-screen televisions, refrigerators, sofas and dining areas. Investigators also reported finding a gym, a golf simulator under construction and luxury vehicles in the complex.
Officials said the residences appeared to house inmates, although prison officials claim they were for staff.

articles.title: Marcos calls on teachers to raise students who are critical thinkers, capable leaders
articles.summary: Marcos calls on teachers to raise students who are critical thinkers, capable leaders

blocks.text: Published September 30, 2026 6:40pm
President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos, Jr on Wednesday called on teachers to raise students who are critical thinkers and competent leaders.
The President made the call during the National Teachers' Month celebration, saying teachers are irreplaceable, more so in the age of Artificial Intelligence (AI).

“When we speak of improving Philippine education, it is essential that we speak of supporting and strengthening the capabilities of the teachers who make learning possible. The most important part of our education system are the teachers. The tools you use may continue to change. Technology, AI will change how our children learn, but it cannot replace a teacher who guides them in deciding what is true, what is important and what is right,” Marcos said.

“I implore you to help shape learners to become critical thinkers who question, discern, make sound decisions and at the same time remaining compassionate and mindful of others. We want capable young Filipinos who will one day lead our communities, our institutions, our country and lead with wisdom, competence and with empathy,” he added.

Marcos said the least the government could do is continue to provide support for teachers, an initiative that has proven to have resulted in gains recently, with the Philippines posting its highest-ever mean scores in the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) in reading, mathematics, and science in 2025.

According to the Department of Education (DepEd), the country recorded mean scores of 373 in science, 371 in mathematics and 367 in reading—up 17 points, 16 points and 20 points, respectively, from its 2022 results.

“Today, we recognize those who are helping to raise that standard ever higher. We have done much already to change the course of Philippine education. I believe that we have made some progress, and the recent PISA result is solid proof. It validates what we are doing and that what we have started has an effect,” Marcos said.

“But of course, we all know much work still remains. There are still gaps in how our teachers are prepared and are developed. Some are assigned to subjects still that are outside their specialization. And while training does not always respond to the realities they face in the classroom, we will try to remedy that. Because teachers do more than just teach lessons. For many of our children, they become second parents in school helping create environments where learners feel safe, supported and cared for,” Marcos added.
The President said remedies would include strengthening school safety and student support together with parents, communities and other partners.

“We will continue to work to make our schools more secure, more responsive to the needs of our learners. At the same time, we continue to improve teacher preparation and professional development throughout your careers,” he said.
He cited the Teacher Education Roadmap 2035 and the Teacher Education Scholarship Program, among other initiatives.
“We want our teachers to have better preparation even before they enter the classroom to have meaningful opportunities to continue learning throughout their careers,” he said.

“Because we ask much from our teachers, we must also give much in return. So together, let us build a Bagong Pilipinas where our teachers are supported to do their best work and our learners are prepared to help shape the country's future,” he added. —VAL, GMA News

Comelec said it open the voter registration from November 2026 to July 30, 2027.

articles.title: Leandro Leviste’s ABS-CBN stake is shrinking, and so is everyone else’s
articles.summary: The expansion of the equity pie alters the corporate math for all outsiders

blocks.text: ABS-CBN Corp.’s stockholders approved on Wednesday, September 30 the P6 billion that will keep the media company going, and Leandro Leviste, who holds the largest stake in it outside the Lopez family, had no hand in putting the deal together. Five parties are providing the money, and he is not one of them.

The Batangas representative’s stake in ABS-CBN, which launched the political career of his mother, former news anchor Senator Loren Legarda, is heavily diluted. He shares the same fate as other public shareholders outside of the Lopez group and allies. His share of the common stock falls from 10% to 3.54%, while his true voting power drops from 4.74% to 2.54%.

The public did not get a chance to buy these new shares. Instead, this is a private deal arranged strictly between the legacy family and friendly incoming capital. Three Lopez family branch holding companies—Crème Investment, Mantes Corporation, and Presta Holdings—are buying primary common shares directly, alongside top holding vehicle Lopez Inc. Entering beside them is strategic turnaround firm I&C Holdings Corp., which is putting in P3.5 billion for 959 million shares to emerge as the single largest common shareholder.

Together, the Lopez family vehicles (around 61%) and I&C (27%) lock up roughly 88% of total voting power. That gap between owning ordinary shares and holding voting power is the whole point: common shares mainly give investors a claim on future profits and dividends, but voting power decides who actually controls the company.

Outside that circle sit public minority investors and Leviste. Without a single share trading hands, their holdings shrink both in value and in their already tiny say in the company as the share pie expands around them.

The capital increase passed on September 30 with 83% of the voting stock behind it, which is what Lopez Inc. at 78.4% and ABS-CBN Holdings at 4.83% add up to. It is likely that the shares being diluted did not vote for it.
The shareholders approved tripling the company’s authorized capital stock to P4.5 billion, and then management directly addressed the changes.

ABS-CBN president and CEO Carlo L. Katigbak defended the move when asked what benefits minority shareholders can expect from the capital increase: “The increase in authorized capital stock will allow the infusion of the P6 billion in equity from our investors. The additional capital is expected to strengthen the Company’s balance sheet, support working capital requirements, and help fund the Company’s turnaround and initiatives. We believe these measures will enhance the Company’s long-term prospects and create value for all shareholders.”
For public minorities who were not invited to take part, company survival and avoiding loan defaults were offered as the reasons for being diluted.

Chairman Martin L. Lopez also made it clear where real control sits. When asked about governance and whether new investors would steer the ship, he drew a firm line: “Lopez Inc., together with its stockholders, Crème, Mantes and Presta, and together with ABS-CBN will continue to determine ABS-CBN’s strategic direction. The new major investor will be consulted and their rights will be respected.”

Leviste moved quickly when he built his stake. On April 30, 2024, his investment vehicle LL Holdings reported holding 75.9 million ABS-CBN common shares and 619,000 Philippine Depositary Receipts (PDRs) through parent firm Countryside Investments, giving him an initial 8.5% of the company.

He gave two reasons for buying, and he gave the warm one first: he timed the purchase around Mother’s Day as a nod to her mother, Loren Legarda, who anchored The World Tonight during his early childhood from 1986 until her 1998 Senate run.

blocks.caption: Loren Legarda’s son gets 8.5% stake in ABS-CBN

blocks.text: “I told her that it was, of course, in time for Mother’s Day,” Leviste said in a May 16, 2024 interview on One News. Asked how she reacted, he replied: “I think that she, like others, would remark that it’s seemingly a risky investment because of the challenges of any media company nowadays but that… even a challenging market at the right price is worth looking, and that it’s very risky and that maybe buying land is a safer bet.”

Pressed on whether the purchase was opportunistic, he agreed: “A large part of ABS’s asset is also in real estate so that’s a good benefit in any company, that your primary business might encounter difficulties but you have some tangible asset underlying the company.” He added: “If there weren’t 10% or so of a company being sold at its all-time low that we wouldn’t have been able to and ended up acquiring that number of shares.”

When Leviste began accumulating in late April 2024, ABS-CBN stock was trading near historic lows in the P3.4 to P4.5 range. Once his initial 8.5% block was disclosed on May 2, the share price surged by 77% to close at ₱7.65 on June 4 as he rounded out his stake to 10%. Across that window, Leviste spent an estimated P300 million to P400 million assembling his position.

In an interview with Bilyonaryo News Channel, Leviste laid out how he snapped up positions being offloaded by foreign investors: “That was more opportunistic, because the price had tanked, and typically companies in the Philippines Stock Exchange don’t have big blocks for sale, but there were foreign investors that were willing to get out at the price… They were actually selling in the market, and then they sold to some other investors, and then those investors were selling in the market as well.”

Part of that came from buying Philippine Depositary Receipts (PDRs). Under Article XVI, Section 11 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution, mass media ownership is reserved 100% for Filipino citizens. Foreign funds cannot hold media shares directly. ABS-CBN Holdings issued PDRs so foreigners could collect cash dividends without holding legal title or voting rights.

Foreign institutional investors had been trimming their exposure to the instruments, and Leviste took advantage of that secondary-market liquidity to accumulate 2.3 million PDRs, holding them alongside 87.7 million common shares as of May 28, 2024. That foreign retreat has only continued since, with foreign-held ABS-CBN PDRs falling further from 41.6 million units at the end of 2025 to 26.4 million units by June 30, 2026.

Post-May 2024, Leviste converted those 2.3 million PDRs into direct common stock. Under local rules, only 100% Filipino nationals can surrender PDRs and take delivery of the underlying media shares. By converting, Leviste turned passive receipts into voting equity, bringing his total holding to 90 million common shares—a clean 10% common block.

blocks.caption: What it took to save ABS-CBN

blocks.text: Headlines in 2024 trumpeted that Leviste owned 10% of ABS-CBN, but the capital structure was engineered long ago to ensure common shares alone could never take control.

ABS-CBN carries two classes of voting stock: listed common shares with a par value of P1, and one billion unlisted voting preferred shares with a par value of just P0.20. Despite costing one-fifth the par value of common stock, each preferred share carries one full vote.

These preferred shares are unlisted, meaning no outsider can buy them in the open market. Private family holding vehicle Lopez Inc. holds 98.71% of them (987 million shares). The remaining around 13 million shares sit across brokerages and personal holdings. It was not a legal wall, but an unlisted closed door: no outsider could ever assemble a meaningful block of preferred shares.
Because voting power is calculated using both share classes combined (899.8 million common shares plus one billion preferred shares), the total voting denominator stood at 1.9 billion shares.

Against that total, Lopez Inc. commanded 78.4% of the vote. Leviste’s 90 million shares gave him 10% of the common stock, but only 4.74% of the total vote. He held no blocking minority, no swing vote, and no unilateral path to a board seat.
Separating economic returns from voting control has long been the setup in Philippine media. Leviste bought the economics because the economics were the only part for sale.

blocks.caption: Why ABS-CBN is still retrenching 200 employees with P6 billion on the way

blocks.text: What Leviste bought a tenth of was an earnings stream that stopped in 2020 and has not returned.

Since Congress denied its broadcast franchise in 2020, ABS-CBN has posted consecutive heavy losses: P6.09 billion in 2024, P4.72 billion in 2025, and another P1.83 billion in the first half of 2026. While content partnerships with GMA, A2Z, and Netflix generated cash flow, heavy operating overhead, talent payroll, and debt service continued to bleed money.
Common and preferred shareholders have received zero dividends since 2020. Cumulative unpaid preferred dividends climbed past P24 million.

Worse, ABS-CBN hit a debt wall: standstill agreements on P8.5 billion in bank debts with BPI and UnionBank had expired, and past-due liabilities were piling up. Without a primary capital injection, the broadcaster faced severe balance-sheet distress.

blocks.caption: Banks, retirees, the business: Where will ABS-CBN’s P6-billion rescue go?

blocks.text: When a listed company needs equity, it typically holds a rights offering, giving all existing shareholders the legal option to buy new shares pro-rata and maintain their percentage stake.

ABS-CBN did not do that. Instead, it sold 1.644 billion primary common shares at P3.65 each to 5 chosen subscribers, citing an exception to the rights offering requirement under Philippine Stock Exchange rules. In a solvency crisis, an open rights offering carries heavy market risk: public shareholders, already nursing paper losses, might refuse to put up fresh cash, leaving the rescue underfunded.
The transaction is not P6 billion in instant bank cash, nor is the money sitting in escrow. Term sheets reveal that ABS-CBN has received P2 billion in upfront deposits upon signing:

items: I&C Holdings paid a P1.5 billion deposit (against its P3.5 billion subscription).
Lopez Inc. paid its full P300 million subscription upfront.
Crème Investment (Geny Lopez line) paid a P100 million deposit (against P767 million).
Mantes Corporation (Manolo Lopez line) paid a P100 million deposit (against P767 million).
Presta Holdings (Prescy Psinakis line) paid no deposit (against P667 million).

blocks.text: The remaining P4 billion is deferred: Crème and Mantes pay their balances “on such date as may be determined by the Board of Directors,” making the remaining cash discretionary rather than an immediate delivery.

Leviste and the other minority shareholders were not invited to participate in the capital raise. In May 2024, he told reporters: “We want to buy more shares. If there will be shares available, then we will buy.” But the new shares were created exclusively for the five subscribers. Outside shareholders were never invited into the room.

blocks.caption: ABS-CBN talks up its ‘new’ future, but its new owners weren’t in the room

blocks.text: The expansion of the equity pie alters the corporate math for all outsiders:
Leviste’s common block falls from 10% to 3.54%, and his voting weight shrinks to 2.54%.

Other retail holders suffer the exact same proportional cut: their collective voting strength drops from 12.02% down to 6.44%. The line marked “Others” in ABS-CBN’s regulatory table reads 318 million shares before and after—the exact same shares, compressed from 16.75% of the company to 8.98% purely because the firm expanded around them. ABS-CBN summarized the impact to the stock exchange in six words: “The public float will be diluted.”

The transaction also closes the door on any outside boardroom clout. I&C Holdings comes in with 959 million common shares—more than 10 times Leviste’s 90 million shares. With I&C and the Lopez family vehicles jointly controlling 88% of total voting stock, Leviste’s ability to act as a swing vote or rally fellow minorities is neutralized.

blocks.caption: ABS-CBN makes room for new owners

blocks.text: Leviste is likely watching this unfold from abroad. The Batangas representative has been out of the country since August, while he and Senator Legarda face a preliminary investigation before the Office of the Ombudsman regarding P10.44 billion in unpaid obligations tied to past solar projects—allegations both have rejected as baseless and politically motivated.
Because his shares are held through LL Holdings Inc., an appointed proxy can still vote his stake. But against an 88% insider bloc, the vote cannot change the outcome.

ABS-CBN gets the P2 billion in initial cash it needs to placate bank creditors and keep producing content. But the recapitalization underscores a familiar rule in Philippine business: in companies shielded by constitutional rules and dual-class voting shares, outside minority shareholders absorb the dilution, while the family and its chosen partners keep the keys. – Rappler.com

blocks.caption: After Gabby sold to Ramon Ang, Piki Lopez is securing the family’s crown jewels

blocks.text: Lala Rimando wrote about Philippine business, and managed newsrooms, including Newsbreak, ABS-CBN, Rappler, and Forbes, for over 25 years. She’s now based in La Union, taking care of her mom with dementia, and working on the multimedia biography of the late John Gokongwei.

articles.title: Commercial plane travelling from Dubai to Israel diverted to Saudi Arabia after distress call
articles.summary: A commercial plane travelling from Dubai in the United Arab Emirates to Israel was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, briefly raising concerns about a possible…

image.caption: A FlyDubai jet, not involved in the diversion to Saudi Arabia, is shown at Dubai International Airport in October 2024. Another of the carrier's planes transmitted an emergency alert Wednesday shortly after takeoff, according to publicly available flight tracking information. (Jon Gambrell/The Assoc

blocks.text: World·New

A commercial plane travelling from Dubai in the United Arab Emirates to Israel was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, briefly raising concerns about a possible hijacking and prompting Israel to scramble warplanes. A regional official briefed on the incident said a fight broke out in the cockpit and apparently involved pilots.
Alert sparks fear of hijacking, but incident involved fight in cockpit among pilots, reports say

A commercial plane travelling from Dubai in the United Arab Emirates to Israel was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, briefly raising concerns about a possible hijacking and prompting Israel to scramble warplanes.

Israeli media, citing security officials, said the incident stemmed from a feud between the plane's two pilots, and everyone on board was safe. The plane landed in Tabuk, a civilian and military base in the kingdom.
The FlyDubai plane transmitted an emergency alert shortly after takeoff, according to publicly available flight-tracking information.
A regional official briefed on the incident said a fight broke out in the cockpit and apparently involved pilots. It wasn't immediately clear what had caused the fight, the official said.
Israel scrambles warplanes

A second official confirmed that Israel had scrambled warplanes, fearing a hijacking of a plane carrying dozens of its citizens. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has warned in recent days of unspecified, escalated security threats.
Both officials spoke on condition of anonymity because the incident was still under investigation.

items: Air traffic control problem disrupts flights across U.K.
Flights resume after ground stops at major U.S. airports, including New York's JFK and ‌LaGuardia

blocks.text: Netanyahu's office later said the situation was under control and Israel was working to bring the passengers home.

Emergency landings for personnel reasons are rare, yet not unheard of. In 2022, two Air France pilots were suspended after fighting in the cockpit on a Geneva-Paris flight, though it did not have to be diverted and landed as planned.
Plane dipped steeply, passengers say

Passengers on the plane told Israel's Channel 12 by phone that they heard shouts from passengers toward the front of the plane who heard the altercation between the pilots, and the plane dipped steeply before landing in Saudi Arabia.
They also said that all the passengers were staying on the plane and that there was a heavy presence of Saudi security forces surrounding them.
FlyDubai is the lower-cost sister carrier of Emirates airlines. The U.A.E. has become a popular vacation destination for Israeli tourists since the countries normalized ties in 2020.
According to Flight Radar, the incident occurred about 2½ hours after takeoff.
FlyDubai later confirmed that Flight FZ 1073, en route to Ben Gurion, experienced an incident and landed safely in Tabuk on Wednesday.
"Our teams are working closely with the relevant authorities," the carrier said. "Further updates will be issued as additional confirmed details become available."

Israelis were targeted in a string of hijackings and airplane attacks by Palestinian militants in the 1960s and 1970s. Israel has not experienced a hijacking in decades but maintains some of the strictest airport security in the world, including often invasive check-in procedures for Israel-bound flights.

articles.title: Palace: Mayors, including Baste Duterte, should know about approved gov't contracts
articles.summary: Davao City Mayor Sebastian Duterte, like any other local chief executive, should not be ignorant of government contracts involving his office or his sister, Vice President Sara Duterte, Palace Press…

blocks.text: Davao City Mayor Sebastian Duterte, like any other local chief executive, should not be ignorant of government contracts involving his office or his sister, Vice President Sara Duterte, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said Wednesday.

“How long has he been a mayor and how does he evaluate the contracts he is signing? Magiging delikado ito kung gagawin din ito ng ibang mga mayor para sabihin, ‘Hindi ko alam na kapatid ko pala ‘yung ka-transaksyon ko.’

(How long has he been a mayor, and how does he evaluate the contracts he signs? This could be dangerous if other mayors do the same and say, ‘I didn’t know that the person I was transacting with was my sibling.')

"For one year, it could be made in good faith. One and a half years would be fine. But if it is going on repeatedly for many years and you still don’t know about it, kailangan siguro mag-isip-isip na (perhaps you need to start thinking about it),” Castro said in a press conference.

Castro was reacting to Mayor Duterte's testimony on Day 31 of the Vice President's impeachment trial, in which he said he was aware that the President and Vice President are prohibited from having business interests under Article VII, Section 13 of the Constitution.
However, he said he did not know that his sister was a stockholder of GenCorp. Industries Inc., which secured P33 million worth of contracts with the Davao City government.

Mayor Duterte also said he would know if there were any irregularities in the contracts, if there were any, and that the 19 contracts won by GenCorp during his sister's tenure as vice president were "not too many."
For two successive years, the Vice President declared GenCorp. as one of her business interests in her 2024 and 2025 Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALNs).
According to Castro, all government leaders should remain alert about transactions involving their offices and should not be unaware or indifferent to potential liabilities.
"So kung may liability si Mayor Baste Duterte, hindi tayo ang maghuhusga dito. Maybe ang taong bayan. Dahil ang pinuno ay hindi dapat manatiling walang alam o walang pakialam,” Castro added.
(If Mayor Duterte has any liability, we will not be the ones to judge it. Perhaps the people will. A leader should not remain unaware or indifferent.)

Castro said it was also puzzling that Mayor Duterte was unaware of his sister's links to GenCorp. when one of the company's shareholders, Jaime T. Cruz, is also a business partner of the mayor and his brother in other ventures.
“It would be better to investigate why he is saying he is unaware of his sister’s links to GenCorp. when one of GenCorp.’s owners is also his business partner,” Castro said.

The prosecution is presenting evidence for Article 2 of the impeachment case against the Vice President, which alleges unexplained wealth arising from her alleged failure to truthfully disclose assets in her SALN and failure to divest from businesses, as required of the President and Vice President under the Constitution.
Good faith defense

Meanwhile, two lawmakers said Baste Duterte cannot invoke a good-faith defense concerning the P33 million government contracts awarded by the city government to GenCorp Industries Inc., a declared business interest of his sister.

Ridon cited that aside from Vice President Duterte listing GenCorp as one of her business interests in her 2024 and 2025 SALN, corporate records submitted to the Securities and Exchange Commission have shown that one of the firm's shareholders, Jaime T. Cruz, is also a fellow shareholder of mayor Duterte and his brother, Davao City lawmaker Paolo Duterte, in other businesses.

“Because of the volume of these documents, they (mayors) cannot be expected to sift through each and every document [of contracts]. [Pero ang] pinag-uusapan po natin, in a broad sense, you are a local chief executive who grants contracts to one of your business associates. You have the same business associate as your siblings, and he (mayor) said Mr. Cruz is a friend of their father,” Ridon said in a press conference, referring to former President Rodrigo Duterte.
“I would say the good faith defense won’t apply here because of these specific facts,” he added.
House Deputy Speaker Paolo Ortega V said the Vice President’s SALN declaration is the "smoking gun."
“The smoking gun here is not the person. The smoking gun is the SALN, these contracts and the documents showing such. That is admission against interest,” Ortega said.

“It is clear that there is a conflict of interest here, because it is the company of your sister who is joining the bid for government contracts, and this same firm won a lot of contracts. Parang napaka-imposible actually na paniwalaan na hindi nila alam ‘yun,” he added.
(It really seems impossible to believe that he was unaware of everything.)
House prosecution panel spokesperson Zia Adiong of Lanao del Sur said GenCorp should have distanced itself from the Vice President.

“While the Vice President’s name is not on GenCorp’s company records, GenCorp should have complained to SEC by now and told them that the Vice President, indeed, has no business interest in the company,” Adiong said.

“They could have asked, why is the vice president misrepresenting us to a point that we are now facing this big trouble at the Senate. But have we heard from them? If she is indeed not involved with GenCorp, this company should have filed a complaint already by now, but there’s none,” Adiong added.

The prosecution is presenting evidence for Article 2 of the impeachment case against the Vice President, alleging unexplained wealth due to alleged failure to truthfully disclose assets in her SALN and failure to divest in businesses as required for the President and Vice President under a Constitutional provision.— MCG, GMA News

blocks.text: Rappler reporter Iya Gozum talks with Bangsamoro member of parliament-elect Naguib Sinarimbo on navigating the politics of building coalitions and the future Cabinet
MANILA, Philippines – Two weeks after the winners of the parliamentary elections in the Bangsamoro were proclaimed, negotiations are underway to build coalitions and the Cabinet.

The election was principally a race between two parties – the Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP) and the United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP). These parties were closely followed by the BARMM Grand Coalition, the party of traditional elites.

Rappler reporter Iya Gozum talks with Bangsamoro member of parliament-elect Naguib Sinarimbo on the work ahead for the newly elected parliament. This includes selecting the chief minister and passing the 2027 budget. Sinarimbo is currently the spokesperson of BFP and was instrumental in the creation of UBJP in 2014.

articles.title: [Be The Good] Does your community want a chat room on Muni?
articles.summary: We need more people leaving the 'old' enshittified internet, and choosing better alternatives

blocks.text: Hello!

You’re probably a member of many online groups already. Perhaps your family has a Viber group where you all like to share photos of get-togethers. Maybe you stay in touch with your high school friends on Telegram, or manage a small book club on Facebook Messenger.

I’m the same. I message various friends, family, and work groups on different messaging platforms. What do most of these platforms have in common? They’re managed by large tech companies which are also heavily invested in algorithms we don’t understand, and AI models that tend to exploit many different communities – from independent artists, to rural villages now occupied by massive AI data centers.

What if I tell you that there are chat rooms inside the Rappler app? What if I told you that we’re offering this chat room space, for free, for groups and communities who value facts and real connection?

Your group could have your own chat room, alongside chat rooms managed by Rappler staff and partners, inside Muni, our space for chat rooms that value facts and information, above virality and profit.

If you’re a subscriber to this Be The Good newsletter, you’re already likely to be the perfect candidate for this. You might be someone who leads, or is active in, groups that value high-quality information, and easy access to news developments and mission-driven work.
What do you get from having a Muni chat room?

items: If your goal is to widen your community’s reach, you can choose to have a public chat room that anyone with an email address can join and send messages to.
If your goal is internal communications with your community, you can have a private chat room where you control the membership.

Muni chat rooms have great community-building features: pinning messages (for announcements or reminders), threading (for more organized communications), notifications (so everyone knows when there’s an important update).
Unique chat room features: you can play YouTube videos inside the chat room, so your members don’t need to hop from app to app. Message, and watch, all in the same space.

Quick access to topnotch information. Journalists, civil society groups, and experts are just another chat room away. You can even request for specific types of Rappler stories to be automatically sent to your chat room, depending on the interests or goals of your community.

Your chat room can exist on your own website. Apart from your chat room being accessible through the Rappler app, you’ll be able to make your chat room visible on your community’s own website, similar to how Philippine news outlets Daily Guardian and SunStar Cebu have their MUNI chat rooms in their websites.

blocks.text: Groups that we think would benefit from having a Muni chat room include other newsrooms (including student-run publications), advocacy groups, hobby-based groups, civil society groups with lots of public events and initiatives, and public interest institutions who want new initiatives and ideas to reach a broader group.
If you’re interested in a Muni chat room for your community, let me know! You can also email community@rappler.com.
We’ll invite you to an exploratory meeting about Muni and how your network or group can benefit from it.

We created Muni because we believe no one should be forced to settle for an internet full of AI slop, disinformation, and exploitative algorithms. We believe there’s another way online. But for this vision to become reality, we need more people leaving the “old” enshittified internet, and choosing better alternatives. (READ: Maria Ressa: Journalists need to build, own technology to protect information integrity)
Muni is that alternative. We hope you can explore it with us!
